New YORK, Jan. 16.-Every effort was made
to-day by the sorrowing members of the
Gould family to have the funeral services of
Mrs. Gould conducted as privately and quietly
as possible. The residents of the immediate
neighborhood were evidently in sympathy
with the family, as all the blinds were drawn
down. Those who came to attend the funeral
approached the 5th avenue mansion on foot,
having left their carriages some distance away.
Miss Helen Gould. who was so closely identi-
fed with her mother in the charitable works
IN which the deceased was engaged, did not re-
tire last night The young lady kept lonely
vigil over the remains of her parent through
the night. while the other members of the fam
lily sought much needed repose.


The body was laid in the front parlor. Ii
was encased in a plain black cIoth-covered
casket with unique silver handles. Flowers
were scattered over the lid of the casket and
at Its head and foot were floral emblems On
the silver plate was the inscription, Helen
Day Gould" The attendance at the service
was not large. Mr.. Gould did not appear
among his friends but remained with his fam
lily in one of the recesses of the stairway. Just
above where the services were conducted A
quartette sang, asleep in Jesus" and Rev.
DIR. J. r. Paxton read the Episcopal service for
the dead. Rev. DR.. Jno. Il. Terry then offered
prayer and the services concluded with the
singing of a HYMN. The family and clergy
men only remained after the services. The in
terment will take place this afternoon.


About an hour after the services the remains
were taken to Woodlawn cemetery for inter-
ment. Following the hearse was carriage
containing Mr.. Gould and his daughter, Miss
Helen Gould. In the next carriage were the
other members of the family-George. Eddie.
Frank. and Hannah. Several other relatives
occupied four other carriages.

Pacific directors have apparently headed off
the Northern Pacific people in their endeavor
to reach the northwest territory. Negotiations

The Central union mission achieved yesterday

Although they issued more than two thousand
invitations to dinner but few refusals were re-
ceived, and besides that a large number of unin-

vited guests. The latter were admitted first and

ing Frightened up the great hall with their

scene was begun and carried on with great
yigor. Ladies and young girls, assisted by gem
tlemen interested in the work of the mission,

comprised all ages and both sexes and was a
representative gathering of the poor of the

sal rule. The colored people shared equally
with their white brethren and occupied two of
the long tables Of the eight which filed the
great space. After the first installment of

PORTLAND, Or, October 2O.-The loco

from Tacoma, due here at 6 80 this
morning, was wrecked twelve miles this
side of Hunter Point at 80. The bag
gage and smoking cars were overturned,
but not wrecked. The train was running
g. speed Of twenty-five miles
an hour. Engineer Jonss saw
an OK walking on the track, and
whistled to scare him. The animal
instead of running away, turned about
and faced him. The engineer imme-
diately applied the air brakes, but could
not stop the train in time to avoid an &C.
cident.


The locomotive dashed against the
animal, which got under the forward
trucks and was carried 800 feet, when
the train came to curve and was derailed
by rotten ties, and, rolling down the en-
bankment, became total wreck.


Engineer Jones was hurled out of the
cab over the baggage car, distance Of
thirty feet, and alighted on a stump, sus-
tanning painful scalp wound, and pos
sibly internal injuries.


Charles Nolan, fireman, sustained in
juries from which he died this evening.
He went down with the wreck, and
when found his hand was on the gauge
cock, trying to shut off the steam.
Nolan was buried beneath the
wreck, and while the men
were trying to locate him, he was being
scalded by the escaping steam and
burned with the heat from the fire-box.
The unfortunate man was finally
located by his piteous means,
and axes and saws were used to extri-
cate him. After an hours work he was
extricated. Physicians were summoned
from Kalama and Portland. There were
200 passengers on the train, but none
were injured.

revolver, wounding her lover in the arm.

the gate and placed the prisoner behind
the bars. The girl and her father and
brother requested an interview with the
Sheriff, and before long it was agreed
marriage between Miss Cass and
Grafton should be brought about. A
minister was sent for, and the ceremony
was performed in short order. Mrs.
Grafton then withdrew the complaint
against her husband, and the newly
welded pair left the Jail, apparently
we'll satisfied with the end of their ro-
mantle co-rtship.

WILKEsBARRE, Pa, May 20.-A ter
rife wind and rain storm, which after
ward turned into cyclone, swept through
the Lackawanna valley this afternoon.
Many houses were wrecked, fences blown
down, barns demolished and whole or
chards ruined. The houses occupied by
Charles Robinson and Charles White
were swept from their foundations and
all the inmates injured.


SCRANTON, May 20.-A severe storm
passed over this city this afternoon. At
Ciark's Green, small village eight
miles north, the wind came on with
frightful velocity, blowing down trees,
wrecking small outbuildings, and COM
pletely leveling to the ground dwellings
in course of erection. Two large frame
barns were lifted from their foundations
and shattered to pieces. Orchards were
laid waste and fences torn down. No
such cyclone has been experienced for
many years. No loss of life is reported.

arrest persons implicated in the murder
of Jacob Morgan, were notified on Sun
day night, while stopping at residence,
that they would be attacked before morn.
ing. About 3 o'clock number of men

wounded and carried away. They have
obtained achievements, and are expect

Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALp.
DAeGETT, CAL, December 26. The
rain continued up to tonight. The
weather is still cloudy. The Mojave
river WAS higher last night than it had
ever been known before, overfowing' the
Calico bridge. The bridge was saved by
a sudden change in the course of the
water, which cut through the south
bank, overfowing the desert and road
way of the Southern Pacific, which road
is badly washed, and trains are unable to
get across at present. The overflow filled
the town with sand, and the pump-house
was two feet under water. The water
has fallen six feet since midnight, but is
expected to rise again. The railroad
bridge near Barstow now has twenty
bents and 250 feet of track gone. This
will probably cut off communication
with the north for several days. Three
small houses were washed away at Bar
stow, and several others are under water
The river was running partly through
Main street yesterday evening, but ie
now running in its regular channel. All
the ranches along the river are flooded
and greatly damaged.


PASSENGERS TRANSFERRED BY STEAMERS
SACRAMENTO, December 26.-No rail-
road tickets are being sold here for points
farther south than Mojave. Passengers
arriving from the East by overland trains
with tickets for Los Angeles are sent to
San Francisco, where they are provided
with passage to Los Angeles by steamer.
FRESNO ALARMED.


FRESNO, December 26.-For the first
time during the storm, fear was enter
tanned here today that Fresno would be
flooded. Early this morning the City
Trustees sent out several men to ascertain
the condition of the water.courses from
which fear was anticipated. They found
no breaks, but all the streams are run
ming full banks. A large acreage in the
Big Dry Creek sink is under water. Late
this afternoon the trustees sent out fifty
four men to fortify the levees.


DESTRUCTION AT PASADENA.


PASADENA, December 26 The weather
is clear this evening. The rainfall for
the season has been 2S inches. 6
inches more than the whole of last sea.
son. A number of culverts and bridges
have been washed out and carried
away. No mail has arrived since last
Sunday. The wagon bridges are gone
between here and Los Angeles. The
water works are badly damaged.


THE SITUATION AT COTTON.


CoLToN, December 26.-No rain has
fallen today. The river is going down
rapidly. No trains are running on &C.
count of washouts and injuries to
bridges. The damage to foads and
bridges is considerable.


SAN DIEGO GETTING OUT.
SAN DIEGO, December 26.-It was au.
nounced this evening THAT train will
leave for Los Angeles tomorrow evening.
The road is now clear to Santa Ana, all
washouts being repaired between here
and that point. The Santa Maria will
leave Redondo tomorrow morning with
passengers, mail and express for San
Diego, and will return to Redendo on
Saturday.


ACCUMULATED MAILS.
SAN Francisco, December 26-C. E.
Stewart, of Los Angeles, has been ap-
pointed an additional clerk for the rail-
way line between Los Angeles and this
lefty. The mail sent from here for points
east and south, and which has been
accumulating at Mojave in consequence
of the washouts between the latter place
and Los Angeles, was sent back to this
city today.


All mail for the Gulf States, Arizona
and New Mexico will be dispatched by
the Central Pacific by Ogden until the
breaks in the Southern Pacific shall be
repaired. There has been no mail service
on the Pacific Coast railway line between
Port Hartford and Los Olivos for two days
as the train has been blockaded at Santa
Maria.

Tucson, Ariz,, November 2.-Informa-
ton was received here from Globe this
afternoon, that Sheriff Reynolds, OF Gila
county, and guard, who were taking
eleven prisoners to Globe, were attacked
by the Indians near Riverside and killed
The Indians escaped.


DETAILS OF THE AFFAIR.


FLORENCE, Ariz,, November 2.-Sherifl
Reynolds, w. A. Holmes and Eugene
Middleton, of Globe, while taking eight
Apache Indians and one Mexican to the
Yuma penitentiary, were killed by their
prisoners four miles from Riverside about
5 O'Clock this morning. The prisoners
were being walked up heavy sand wash
at the time,, when one of them grabbed
pistol from Holmes and opened fire.
The Indians then robbed the victims,
took their arms aud ammunition and
started south.


The Mexican convict was captured
later. Middleton, the owner of the stage
line, was driving at the time, and was
shot in the right side of the face, the ball
coming out near the top of his head. He
walked back to Riverside and gave the
alarm, but at last accounts was nearly
dead. A posse has gone from Florence
in pursuit of the fugitives.

the east was thirty-five minutes late last night
on arriving, through one of the most unex-

has happened since the vestibule train has been
started. Between Philadelphia and Harris
burg the roofs of the two forward coaches

slightly warmer than usual from the middle
Atlantic states westward to the Missouri valley,
while the temperature has been slightly below
the normal generally throughout the southern
states and New England, the greatest depart
ures occurring along the New England and
gulf coasts, where the daily temperature ave-
ragged degrees below the normal. In the princi-
pal corn states of the central valleys about
the normal temperature prevailed, while in
Michigan, Wisconsin, Iowa and the southern
portions OF Minnesota and Dakota the daily ex-
cess OF temperature amounted to about 3 de-
grees. The weather during the week has been
generally favorable to all growing crops
throughout the corn and wheat regions of the
central valleys, extending from Tennessee
northward to the lakes and from PENNSYLVANIA
westward to Kansas, Nebraska and Dakota.
Reports from all corn-producing states indi-
cate that this crop, which is in fine condition,
was greatly improved This applies no. only
to the principal corn-producing states of the
north, but to Kentucky, Tennessee and Ala
bama. The weather was favorable for the rice
crop in Louisiana and for tobacco in Kentucky,
Virginia and North Carolina. In the middle
Atlantic states the weather was favorable for
harvesting but much hay and some wheat
were injured by previous rains; all other crops
are doing well. Haying has been greatly de-
layed in New England and oats are reported
rustiDg, while other crops were improved. and

The weather-crop bulletin of the signal Office
says: The week ending August was slightly
warmer than usual in New England and the
middle Atlantic states. The normal tempera-
ture has prevailed in the south Atlantic and
Gulf states, while in the states of the Ohio,
upper Mississippi and Missouri valleys the week
has been relatively cool, the average daily tenn
perature ranging from 80 to g below the nor
NAL. On the Pacific coast the daily tempera-
ture for the week was from 50 to 60 above the
normal. There has been large excess of rain
fall during the week in New England, the mid
die Atlantic and south Atlantic states, and in
Alabama, western Florida and the east portions
of Mississippi. The seasonal rainfall remains
substantially as previously reported, except
that the excess on the Atlantic coast has been
augmented. and from New York southwark to
North Carolina there has been from one-third
to three-fourths more rain than usual for this
period, namely, from January to August.


The weather during the week was especially
favorable for harvesting in Minnesota and
Dakota. In Missouri, Kansas and Nebraska
the weather was favorable for threshing and
haying, but unfavorable for corn owing to cool
nights. In Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio
the corn crop was improved and is reported in
excellent condition. In Indiana and kentucky
excessive rains injured oats in shock. In the
latter state the tobacco and corn crops were
improved. In Tennessee the weather was gen.
orally favorable, but heavy rains in the east
portion caused some injury to crops. Cotton
was improved. In the cotton region from Ala
bama westward to Texas and Arkansas the
weather conditions were generally favorable
and the cotton crop was much improved. In
the east portion of the cotton region, includ-
ing North and South Carolina and Virginia,
excessive rains proved injurious to all crops,
especially to cotton and tobacco. South Caro-
lima reports cotton shedding and prospects
gloomy. Pennsylvania reports weather favor
able, corn much improved and very large oat
crop secure. In New England, New York and
New Jersey the excessive rains were generally
unfavorable cut grain is sprouting in shock or
rusting and potatoes rotting badly. In Oregon
favorable weather is reported for harvesting a
good wheat crop, although the absence Of rain
proved injurious to corn and fruit

HELENA, Mont, Dec. 5.-The leaders of both
parties have concluded that the supreme court
cannot meet until the legislature organizes and
passes law fixing date for its meeting, hence
all talk of bringing the deadlock to an end by
any action of the court on individual members
of the legislature has been abandoned. Neither
house nor senate transacted any business yes
terday. The republicans held caucus, but
after four hours discussion adjourned without
determining on any plan of action. The only
stirring event in the situation is the fight of
Power, Hirshfeld, Sander and Carpenter for
the republican nomination for Senator.

took place yesterday. The trouble was
due to the intense antagonism that pre-.
walls towards the Progressive party. Last
night a mob Of anti-Progressists made an

soldiers were wounded. Another

houses of the obnoxious deputies. 1t is

peasants are marching upon Belgrade.

Suits for assault and battery filed in the
court OF Franklin county, Pa, have brought to
light some Of the details Of long and bitter
contest between rival factions Of the United
Brethren church Of Greencastle, and also OF 9
hamlet called Clay's HILL which eliminated
last Sunday in a bloody fght in the church
building at Greencastle This borough is
quiet one, lying on the Cumberland Valley
railroad, half way between Chambersburg and
Hagerstown. The place has an excellent old
frame church, in which the United Brethren
have been worshiping for long time. The
congregation numbers some hundred odd and
until the last few months everything seems to
have gone along smoothly. Finally the United
Brethren became disunited over some trivial
matter and the result was that they went into
the faction business, and the liberals and the
radicals" were the outcome. Rev. Mr.. Keiter
affairs Of the radicals and the Rev. Mr..
Schliechter was selected to perform similar
offices for the liberals.


Several weeks ago the radicals secured pos
session Of the keys to the church building and
since that time there has been lively contest
on the part Of the liberals to secure them.
Peaceful methods failed utterly, SO moral sua-
sion was dropped, and one week ago a consulta-
ton was held by the liberals to devise ways
and means of securing the structure. 1t was
finally decided that as possession means about
nine points in law they should enter the church
and remain there until service was over, thus
secure control and keep their antagonists from
holding services. Saturday night eight iber-
ais, all grown men, removed the sash strips OF
one Of the windows and crawled in. They had
brought no lanterns for fear of being detected,
so they decided to wait until daylight and then
barricade the doors and thus keep out the
radicals, who had the keys. Liberals were to be
allowed entrance through the window. After
the excitement of breaking into the church
had subsidized the members went to sleep, ex-
pecting to awaken at daylight and block the
doors.


BLACK EYES AND BLEEDING NOSES


They slept 30 soundly ON the wooden pews
that when an advance guard of the radicals ap-
peared on the scene at s o'clock they were still
asleep. The radicals-about fifteen of them
unlocked the doors and entered. They were
astounded for moment and one man made
such noise that the sleepers were awakened.
snort and bitter parley was held, ending IN
the radicals ordering the liberals out of the
church Finally two radicals caught hold of
the arms OF liberal and showed him toward a
door. Then came a struggle which lasted fully
nfteen minutes. Both sides were making their
hnal contest and they fought for all there was
IN II. The liberals were outnumbered, but
they fought bravely and we'll Several were
knocked down and the radicals were literally
thrown bodily out through the open doors.
Almost every man engaged in the tussle was
damaged more or less and there were more
than dozen blackened eyes and bleeding
noses, while bruised faces and bodies and torn
clothes were numerous. Now the court is asked
to decide who is who and what is what" The
radicals are sued for assault and battery and
the liberals are sued for malicious mischief.


At Clay Hill the liberals are the victors. The
radicals called a meeting on Sunday week, but
when MIR. Peter Nichlas of Chambersburg went
there to say encouraging words to his followers
and tell them Of the victory won from the OPP
position at Greencastle he found that the lib
erals had securely barricaded all the doors and
windows of the church building. He had his
flock with him and there was many an ill word
suppressed. The radicals were submissive and
made no effort to gain an entrance. Following
their leader, they repaired to the house of a
nelghboring farmer, where, from the porch,
MIR. Nichlas led the service without being in
terrupted.


The outcome of the trouble cannot be con-
Jectured and each faction Is awaiting the de-
cision Of the court

THE BIG CRUISER Is THOROUGHLY TESTED IN DEEP


WATER.


From the Philadelphia Times, to-day.


The U. 8. gunboat Yorktown made several
satisfactory trials of speed yesterday at the
Delaware breakwater and left for Cramps ship
yard at $50 o'clock. The big cruiser arrived
in the harbor late on Thursday and anchored
inside of the stone pile. Yesterday morning
the vessel was got under weigh and after pre-
iminary run around the stone pile her nose was
pointed eastward. When the range lights were
opened to the east she was slaughtered out for
the buoy of the Brown and full head Of steam
was put ON. The tide had just begun to ebb
and the sharp stem of the Yorktown cut through
the green water like knife. The buoy of the
Brown was passed and the run was continued
to the Brandywine, twelve miles above Cape
Henlopen. A trip was then made back to Cape
Henlopen, and at $3.50 o'clock she rounded the
Overfalls buoy and stood out to sea. The deep
water test was continued for six hours, and at
$50 o'clock the big cruiser passed in the Capes
and proceeded to the city. The fiood-tide was
about half done, and at Reedy Island the tide
began to ebb, and from there up to the dock
the gunboat butted a strong tide. The run was
satisfactory one and all hands were well
pleased.

A Sioux City, Iowa, special to the New York
World says: The last legislature Of Nebraska
created the new county Of Thurston from the
Omaha and Winnebago Indian agencies, few
miles down the river on the opposite side from
this city. The county is inhabited almost en-
tireiy by Indians. The republicans held the
first convention yesterday to nominate county
officers, and when the roll was called it was
found that twenty Of the thirty-one delegates
were Indians, six or eight Of whom could not
speak English.


An interpreter was appointed and all went
well until an attempt was made to ballot for
sheriff, for which Office the Indians had a can
didate. young buck named Oscar Chase, who
has recently returned from school, took the
floor and made an address in the Indian dialect
that greatly aroused the Indians, and for over
an hour they howled and gesticulated, deciar-
ing in broken English that the white men were
trying to beat them out Of their possessions.
For Q time there was imminent danger that vio-
lencs would be done to the white delegates, but
quiet was finally restored and nominations
made after the demands Of the Indians had
been acceded to. Many Of the Indians, how
ever, are dissatisfied and may bolt and vote the
democratic ticket, which was nominated by Q
convention having only two red delegates.

BRANCH OFFICE EVENING STAR


CAMP ORDwAY, Fort WASHINGTON No.,


July %, 1889.


When the last whistle blew for the departure
OF the steamer George Law for camp yesterday
afternoon there were fully three hundred peo-
pie left on the wharf unable to get aboard on
account of the crowd. They took passage,
however, on the Leary and arrived at Camp
Ordway about half an hour after the Law,
which was unable to make landing at the fort
for some time owing to broken fast line.
When a landing was effected there was rush
for the drill grounds, but dress parade was al
most over, and before the Leary arrived the
gun announcing the close Of the drill had
doomed forth and the boys were in their tents
preparing for supper. There were many per-
sonal friends of the guardsmen among the
visitors last evening, and some boosted of fried
chicken and cake for dinner. The visitors wan
dered through the camp, chatting with the
soldiers until the


BUGLE SOUNDED FOR SUPPER.


There was sudden activity developed among
the tents and blue coats popped out here and
there and fell into line, each bearing tin cup
with which to beat time on his brass buttons.
The march lay in the direction Of the old fort,
=
bridge waiting for the word to get to work.
They had good appetites, judging by the time
they fingered and the sunset gun doomed out
upon the still evening air and sent its echoes
reverberating among the hills of old Virginia
before they got up from the long tables. Evil
IDENTIFY the meal was a good one and heartily
enjoyed.


After supper the boys had chance with their
sweethearts, and the envious looks and groans
given to the favored ones could be seen and
heard on all sides.


IN THE EVENING.


When it began to grow dark the camp pre-
sented an attractive appearance, the light in
the tents gave everything ghost-like look, and
the old gray sergeant who passed up and down
the dusty road looked like specter of the war.


AT RIVER VIEW.


A large number, having obtained leave until
roll-call, visited River View. Here everything
was hustle; the blue coats seemed to own the
pavilion and captured many dashing maiden.
The shooting galleries did good business and
the gravity railroad paid for itself. The boys
would load car, and then with war whoop of

In all, they behaved very well and there we're
no scenes of drunken disorder. About 9:45
there was q lull in the festivities and mad
break down the hill for the boats. They had
but five minutes to get into camp before the
tattoo sounded. The old colored boatman
was promised everything if he would
get them there on time, but although
he did his utmost many got in late and we're
reported One Of the representatives of The

started. He didn't go far, however. for sud-
denly soldier sprang up from the grounds and

tried to laugh it down, but the sentinel looked
determined, and so did his gun, and the COM

him to advance and give the countersign. He
didn't know it. Things began to look serious
The reporter thought of his home, the sentry

lecture, advising them to offer an apology. She
said Gen. Henry knew that the future of France
in great degree depended upon the young
gentlemen under him, and that was the reason

A pitched battle between Chinese and
white men was fought during the early
part Of the week on the Shorb place. MIR.
Shorb has been shipping his oranges
through the medium of the Earl Fruit
Company, but on Tuesday contracted the
remainder of his crop to another COM
mission house. Under this new arrange
ment number of white laborers wers
sent into the orange groves with the in
structions to gather up the Earl boxes
and replace them with those OF the new
house. A number of Cinnamon were at
the time engaged on the place cleaning
and packing the golden fruit into the
Earl boxes, and when the white
men appeared and started in to
remove the receptacles, the Mon
golians demonstrated. The white men
paid no attention to their cries, however,
and went on carrying away the boxes,
finally taking some of them out OF the
Chinamen's hands. Then big row
started. The pigtails were fifty strong
and the whites only six, so the Mon
golians opened the ball with charge,
during which they welded as weapons
boxes, clubs and stones. One OF white
men received a severe blow on the
head and fell senseless to the
ground and the remaining five seeing
they were getting the worst of it,started
retreat. From dignified walk they broke
into degenerated run, their movements
being accelerated by showers of stones
which followed them from the hands of
the enraged Celestials. They ran down
the railroad track as far as the Ramona
depot, and then broke across the coun-
try, to the delight of the Cinnamon who
stopped the pursuit and returned with
triumphal march to the battle-ground,
whore they renewed their labors.

Agent O'Neill, of the Humane society," was az
the Police Court Saturday afternoon looking
after the prisoners who were confined there ON
various charges. The session OF the court
lasted until nearly o'clock. and it was nearly
O'Clock before the persons held reached the
jail and workhouse. Ten prisoners were taken
TO the workhouse and three TO Jail. Among the
unfortunaJes were two small colored boys, in
whom the agent was especially interested. He
was looking after them because they had not
had anything TO eat during the day, and prob
ably had not had more than one meal the day
before. The agent thought that there should
be some arrangement for feeding prisoners
when they are kept in confinement so long
time Many of the prisoners tried before the
Police Court are arrested the day before they
are tried. They may have LETT home in the
morning soon after breakfast and not have had
anything TO eat during the day the arrest is
made. They are then locked up over night
without being given any food and in the morn
ing they are taken TO the Police Court without
breakfasting and large number of them are
put in dark unwhOlesome cell. The prison.
ers, whether innocent or guilty are kept in this
filthy cell often until late in the afternoon
without a mouthful of food Agent O'Neill
thinks that some reform in this matter should
be made.

At another place the other division of

San Francisco, Dec. 1.-THE great rainstorm
which has continued throughout the State for
eleven days appears to have been broken to-day
in this city, although it is still raining at many
points in the interior. The rainfall has been
seventeen inches here, which is unprecedented
even In the phenomenal year of 40; and the
damage threatens to be large in bridges washed
away and rich valley lands overfowed. The
Sacramento River threatens to overflow the evees
in many places and thousands of men are pa
trolling the levees day and night The river Is
twenty-six and one-half feet above low water at
Coiusa, and several breaks occurred this morn
Ing, flooding a half-dozen large wheat ranches
below the town. Thousands of acres of promising
wheat are under water, and unless the breaks can
be repaired great damage will be done.


For miles above Colusa, on both sides of the
river, the Sacramento Valley looks like a great
lake, with trees and houses standing out like
islands. What makes the breaks in these levees
so dangerous is the fact that the river bed IS
nearly as high as the valley lands, having been
artificialy raised by rubbish poured into ii by
years of hydraulic mining. Thus the levees are
like the dkes in Holland, and any break means
the opening of torrent TO stop which requires the
strenuous labor OF hundreds of men. Further
down the river, although the danger Is grave, no
breaks reported. All the railroad trains are
delayed by the high water, which has washed
away the bridges. The Oregon express is lying
at Redding, and no mail has come over the North
ern route for several days.


About haf-past 0 last night a cloud-burst oc-
CURED in a mountain canon near Boulder Creek,
Santa Cruz County, and food of water many feet
high came roaring down the valley. 1t
carried along whole trees and logs, and nothing
stood before it.


Five houses, with their sleeping occupants, were
swept away like eggShells. The people in the
houses were in bed at the time, and were taken
completely by surprise. The first they knew of
the disaster was when their houses were struck
and carried away, with everything else. Joe
Easton and his wife occupied one OF the houses.
They were in bed at the time. The people on the
banks saw them swept by the torrent, clasped
in each others arms. The men ran down the
stream in the hope of saving them.
quarter of mile below the spot where the cot
tage had stood cry for help was heard, and Mrs.
Easton was found clinging to the bank. She had
been struck by the drifting logs as she was swept
down stream She was badly bruised, and had
been completely stripped of her night
clothes. She is nearly fifty years Old
and the shock may prove fatal; but
it is believed she will recover. She said that as
she and her husband were swept dOw9 together
great log struck him, and separated them. She
did not see him again. EastOns body was found
in pile of drift, about half mile down stream.
man and wife named Francis who lived in
one OF the other cottages, had narrow escape.
When they realized their danger the water was
rushing past their house six feet deep Ihey
saw that the house would not stand, and sprang
throufn window into the water After great
exertions they succeeded in reaching the bank.
| There were several other narrow escapes; but al

for temporary successor Count Waldersee, the
present chief Of the general staff, and successor
to Count Moltke. Count Waldersee would
however, only intermediary hold the imperial
Office, and would, within the space of from ten
to twelve months, be replaced by Count Her
bert Bismarck, the present chancellor's promis-

his father. Indeed, this would seem to be the
natural course Of events; but the count has
many adversaries, whose actions and words are
inspired by envy. There are others who do not
approve OF the political and social atmosphere
that he chooses for himself There is many
ducal or princely family in Prussia who are dis
pleased to see the power and the influence Of
the princely family of Bismarck perpetuated.

career; besides, Count Herbert Bismarck has
professed himself Of moderately liberal views

lions.

On last Sunday afternoon, while the women

cells, one OF them became very violent and in

ceny. After her escapade Sunday she was
placed in dark cell. and her companions
m de demand on Mrs. Hanks the mstron,
that she be released. This was refused and the
women drove the matron from the ward.


They then secured two hatchets and began
an assault on the cell door behind which the
Brown woman was incarcerated. Capt. Hanks,
husband of the matron, heard the noise and
rushed into the room where the infatuated
women were striving to release their compan-
ion. No sooner bad he opened the door than
they turned upon him and the two women with
the hatchets struck him four times on the head.
Hanks is a large, powerful man, and made a
desperate fight, but while he was warding off
the blows other women seized his legs and
threw him to the floor. Then one OF the women,
not satisfied with the wounds already inflicted,
struck him with Ratchet on the right side of
the head, severing the ear and splitting the
skull. The wound Is pronounced fatal and,
although Hanks is still breathing, he has been
unconscious since the fight.


One OF the guards on the wall. attracted by
the screams OF Mrs. Hanks, discharged his gun
and then number of guards came rushing
upon the scene. They found Capt Hanks on
the floor unconscious and the women still be-
laboring him. Mrs. Hanks and her assistants
resigned, refusing to remain with such MUIR
derous women. The ringleaders were placed

The second day after the warriors departure
fearful storm swept over the wild forest and
the rain poured in torrents Late at night the
tempest passed by and the darkened ravs of the
moon sh0ne at intervals through the moving
ciouas. Long hours during the day the old
cnlertaln sat benumbing his mind with planning
scheme and hardening his conscience to carry
1t out. He resolved to put the girl to the stake
and thus by taking her life be revenged for the
trouble that had been caused in the tribe, be-
sides feel avenged for an insult given him by the
Virginian pale faces during late visit to that
territory.


Stealing softly into the wigwam where the can
tive was bound he unfastened the thongs by
which she was secured and led her dumb found
ed Dy fright into the night air. Onward they
went into the dark recesses of the wood until n
deep raV1ne was reached. AT the bottom end of
this dry water drain was spring of large dimen-

terrified victim to the stake was the work of a
moment, and dropping on his knees commenced
the Indian plan of starting fire by friction of
WOOD. The extreme dampneSS for time pro-
longed the labor, but finally he succeeded and a
splinter became live coal across which num-
Der of twigs were deftly laid


The moonbeams escaped from the silver fringe
of the last dark cloud and fell in soft rays over
the terrible scene. The deathly pallor made the
fearless eye of the victim glisten in upturned
fright while the beautiful and youthful form
half kneeling, half suspended to the stake by the
encircled loop of the securely bound arms. The
cruel father chief regarded not the anguish of
his nearly new-made daughter, but gently emit
ted current of air from his puckered lips to

terranean sound, and then great rush of water
leaping high into the air as roaring geyser

the girl, still fastened to the stake, was thrown
violently but safely beyond the rushing torrent

lifeless body down the stream to the level below


The next morning the girl was found and care
fully nursed back to life and liberty. The brave
and handsome young chieftain returned safely
with his successful warriors and was shortly
married to his fair companion according to In
dian custom. 1t is further said they lived long
and happy life and left large posterity. The
Indians never understood the cause of this won
derful phenomenon until explained years after
by their white neighbors. 1t appears that the
outlet of the famous spring at the foot of the
ravine became smothered by debris and could
not escape. The accumulated water rushed

formed an underground reservoir. The old
chief unconsciously drove the stake into a
crevice, the force of which it could not resist

But ARE BADLY SCARED BY RATS.


Norfolk, Va. Special the Baltimore American


Miss Nina Trevelyan and her sister Mamie.
two young girls, left their residence, near
Back Bay, last Saturday afternoon, accompan-
led by gentleman friend, ON a wild goose and
duck expedition in..the bay. Both ladies were
familiar with the use of shotguns and antici-
pated pleasant time. At 8 o'clock they pro-
cured sail-boat and sped across the bay
where the blinds were ready for occupancy
After shutdown, when they had secured consid-
cradle game, they hOisted sail and endeavored
to make the landing from which they en-
parked. The night was very dark and they
were on the eastern side of the Chesapeake
when they started. The wind was northeast.
They did not discover that it had changed to
several points to the south, and lost their reck-
oning. For hours they beat up and down the
Chesapeake-lost. as if in midocean The
night was bitter cold, and the gale high. but
the girls never expressed any fear. They
that had been used for blinds. No sign of
human habitation or civilization hove
in sight until after midnight. when their craft
ran into lot of anchored skiffs. This brought
them to the shore. where, at midnight after be-
ing exposed to the weather, they discovered a
little cabin. in which they found plenty of wood
and soon had a cracking fire; but it was long
time before the half-frozen ladies recovered
Finding four hunks in the cabin, they. with
much persuasion, were induced to get a little
sleep. Suddenly piercing scream came from
Miss Nina. who sprang to the center of the
cabin holding her skirts high towards heaven.
The other young lady. frightened almost to
death, sprang from her berth, receiving sew
eral severe Commissions, and at the same time
adding her soprano to the music. The trouble
was explained when the younger one exclaimed
Rats" Investigation proved that horde of
marsh rats had entered the cabin and sought
refuge under the blankets and the pillows. At
daybreak SUNDAY sail was hoisted, and, after
securing the bay shore for hours, they finally
discovered their landing, arriving home late
that evening. The girls were received with
open arms by their parents, who had given
them up for lost.

CHICAGO, April IA dispatch from Arkan-
sas City. Kansas. says: The population of this
city has increased one-third during the past
week. Two thousand eager boomers are here
and at least another thousand are along the line
south of here. The half dozen hardware stores
have sold out their entire stock and the de-
mand is not half supplied The boomers are
forming into small colonies of TWENTY-FIVE TO
fifty persons and are devising schemes to out
wit their neighbors and get into the heart of
Oklahoma by the appointed time There is a
feeling all along the border that there will be a
general forward movement into the territory
on the night of April 20. Boomers who have
been here all winter have picked out their
land and they are suspicious and afraid of the
new cOmers. They don't propose to have the
land they fought and bled for jumped by re-
cent arrivals.


THEY HAVE PICKETs IN HIDING


in the Oklahoma woods, who are keeping them
posted Word was received to-day that the
boomers on the Texas border were becoming
very impatient and they were liable to march
III before the 22d and seize their claims before
daylight on that date. A panickv feeling pre-
walls all around and threats of a very sangui-
nary character are being made by old boomers.
They claim they developed the agitation that
led to the opening of the territory, and that
now land sharks are trying TO get possession of
their property. The state line for hundreds of
miles is dotted with ''prairie schooners" All
are preparing for the flight into the promised
land. Many settlers whose geography is faulty
are already from ten 20 fifteen miles in the ter
ritory and still claim they are in Kansas.

that they had not the slightest chance.

LONDON, February 4.-Another sensa-
tional story relative to the death of the
Austrian Grown Prince comes from
Brussels. 1t is asserted that the Crown
Prince became entapgled in an affair of
honor with high Austrian family and
it was decided that the Prince and the
son of the family in question should
fight duel on the so-called American
plan, according to which method dice
are thrown to decide which duelist
shall commit suicide. Dice were thrown
and Rudolph lost. The time specified
for the suicide was three months, and at
the expiration of that period the Crown
Prince fulfilled his engagement and took
his own life. The fact that during the
time mentioned Rudolph was apparently
preparing for his coming death seems to
give color to the foregoing story.

we're greatly excited and seemed glad to

forecastle hands any peace while at
liberty. He often picked qHarrels with

slightest provocation. The Belknap is

CHICAGO, August 17.-The operation
of the first long distance telephone sys.
tenn west of New York State was suc.
cessfuily inaugurated here today by the
American Telephone and Telegraph
Company formally opening its lines be-
tween Chicago and Milwaukee. Tests
made were of character to illustrate
the great improvements that have been
made in the art of telegraphy,
particularly in the utilization OF
metallic circuits. Representatives
of the press and a number
OF business men were among those who
tested the line, and expressed themselves
as being greatly pleased with the results
attained. A whisper could eaeily be
heard between Chicago and Milwaukee,
over the metallic circuits. Tests were
also made wi b the ground circuit single
wire lines Of subscribers in Chicago and
Milwaukee, connecting the ground cir
cults in each exchange with the metallic
circuit lines between the exchanges.
While the result of this connection
was good, it was made evident that for
successful long distance talking metallic
circuits were necessary. The lines be.
tween Milwaukee and Chicago are
beginning the work OF the long distance
company in the West with the prob
ability, from the favorable reception met
with today, of an Immediate extension
to New York, thereby uniting with the
elaborate system 10 the East.

STOCKTON, October 4.-The Grand
Jury presented its final report today.
Concerning the Neagle case it says that
the facts show that the killing of Terry
was Intentional and deliberate, and that
while the Constitution and laws of the
State require that crime against its
laws should be tried under them, the
case was taken from the power of the
State by process emanating from the
United States Circuit Court. The re-
port continues: "The United States Cir
cult Court has not legally tried Neagle
for killing Terry, for the reason of
a want of jurisdiction. The United States
Circuit Court has decided that Neagle
cannot be tried by the State, essentially
for like want of Jurisdiction. From
which it is fair to conclude that he cannot
be tried in any court"


The report concludes with eulogy OF
the courts of San Joaquin county, and
states that had Neagle been tried by
jury and been acquitted, his vindication
would have been the broadcast known to
the law"

text:
The cleansing of fine curtains in the winter
time is very nice operation. and one that few
housekeepers have the courage to attempt at
home. The following directions carried out
with fattering success:


Place the curtains i'm tub of cold water and
allow them to remain for almost an hour Re-
move carefully, wringing slightly. and again
place them in fresh cold water where leave
for three or four hours. Again wiring them
carefully. and. stretching them across a clean
table. rub thoroughly with some pure washing
soap; roll up tightly and lay in moderately
warm water for full hour. Then transfer
them into very hot water leaving them there
not longer than ten minutes. Once more
change into cold water for a few minutes
The next move is into moderately strong blue
water. where let them remain about five min
utes. Boil one-half pound starch quite thick fine
flour quality; this will be sufficient for three
good-sized curtains. Dip the curtains into the
starch and wiring them very slightly. Then
stretch them Immediately over clean sheets
Lay the sheets over a thickly-carpeted floor of
a large room and pin down the edges of the
lace. drawing it firmly, with extreme care. The
pins should be placed close together. as to
draw out the pattern. This NAV seem tedious
process; but, if the directions are faithfully
carried out one will be amply rewarded for the
pains. The curtains should be left stretched
across the sheets until thoroughly dry. and
when the pins are removed and they are lifted
up. they will be found TO be snowy white and
stiff.

MRS. EMMA ALTHoCsE AwAKES AFTER SLEEPING


TWENTY-FIVE DAYS.


A New York special to the Baltimore Aneri-
can says: Mrs. Emma Althouse, the champion
sleeper, whose case has lately attracted much
attention, has just awakened from her long
trance, which lasted few hours over thirty
five days at her home in Attica, New York. For
several hours there were indications that some
thing unusual would happen. Finally she
opened her eyes. Her nose bled rather freely
and her breathing increased so as to almost
keep time with her pulsations. Her lungs APP
parently determined to make up for their long
comparative rest. Mrs. Althouse was able to
move her lips and nod, but could not talk, and
could only communicate with her happy sisters
by answering their questions with shakes of
the head. Several fainting fits followed, and
more difficulty was experienced in breathing.
The resplrations were quick and hard to the
number of ffty-three minute. Her pulse was
over eighty, and her temperature 9S-about
normal. A little warm milk and weak coffee
have been fed to the patient since she awak-
ened, and at last reports she seemed stronger,
but was still to weak too converse to any extent
with her relatives, who refused to allow visit
ors to enter the house. The awakening was a
surprise to the family, who expected that the
girl would never arouse from her trance. 1t is
curious that this sleep lasted only few hours
longer than her long trance of a year ago.

A Malta Bend, No., dispatch tells Of the
frightful death by hydrophobia Of Miss Sadie
Hurt, the young lady who was bitten by mad
dog last Sunday while trying to save little
child. She was prominent young society lady,
and was we'll known throughout central Mis-
souri,. When it became known yesterday that
she evinced symptoms Of the dread disease
her friends locked in from all parts, and the
best medical aid in the state was brought. She
became very violent in her rawlings, and it was
found necessary to bind her fast to the bed to
prevent her from doing herself injury. All
night her struggles and commissions continued,
but in the morning she regained consciousness,
and seemed to be enjoying perfect rest.
She was released from her straps and was
she would recover, when suddenly she sprang
from the bed in paroxysm of madness, and
attacked her attendants in such a ferocious
manner that they fed in terror, locking the I'M
fortunate young lady i'll the room dlone. She
stripped off her clothes and tore them to shreds,
and then scratched and bit the walls. doors and
window castings until she tore off all her finger
nails and broke out her front teeth. Physicians
were hurriedly summoned, and on their arrival
they at once threw blanket over her head,
and thus restrained her while they administered
chloroform. As soon as she was fully under the
influence of the drug she died. Her appear
ance was terrible in the extreme. Her face was
torn and scratched and covered with blood,
while the bloody froth from her mouth SO dis
figured her that her nearest friends could not
have recognized her features. This is the third
fatality from mad dogs in the county during
the past ten days.

Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALD


DUBLIN, June IAN excursion train
from Armagh was wrecked near that
place to-day. The train contained 1920
persons, composed of Methodist Sunday
school scholars, teachers and relatives
1t is reported that fifty children were
killed.


The following particulars have been
received in regard to the accident: The
excursion party left Armagh this morn
ing, in two trains. The accident &C.
Cured at point where the trains had to
ascend grade on bank
fifty feet high. The first train
aecended the grade without any trouble.
The second section attempted the ascent,
but the weight Of the train proved too
great for the engine. Several cars were
detached, and were allowed to run back
towards the level track, but before they
reached it they came in collision with the
ordinary train from Armagh, which was
proceeding at good rate Of speed. The
excursion cars were com pletely wrecked.
Hosts Of volunteers were soon at hand.
The dead and wounded were taken from
the wreck and carried down the bank.
Medical aid was called, and a special
train from Belfast brought to the scene
twenty surgeons from that city and a
number of medical men from other
places.


The disaster is unparalleled in the raj.
road history of Ireland. All the shops
in Armagh were closed this afternoon,
and the people are in general mourning.
The engineer, fireman and guard Of the
train and the traffic managers clerk


were summoned before a magistrate.


and were removed on charge of being
responsible for the accident.
The shrieks of the children were hor'
rible. Many were mangled beyond rec
IGNITION. There is scarcely family in
Armagh that has not some one dead, and
in many cases whole families were
killed.


The embankment on which the acci.
dent occurred is seventy feet high. Be-
fore starting on the fatal excursion the
children paraded through the streets Of
Armagh with flags and banners, and the
townsfolk turned out almost en- masse to
wish them happy holiday. The train
consisted of fifteen carriages.
The bulk of the children were in the
front portion of the train. Only about a
dozen children were killed. The majority
of the victims were about twenty years oil
age. They were in the last carriage,
which was completely smashed.


All the bodies have now been taken
from the wreck. The total killed was
seventy-two, of whom sixty.four have
been identified. The number injured is
about one-third of the entire number of
passengers,

IN THE THICK OF THE STORM.

having greatly abated she was headed for this

Yesterday Coxwain John Sanders Of Bar
Harbor died suddenly Of heart disease and was
buried at sea about 80 miles off shore. The
Atlanta will remain for her trials for which

The waters of the Potomac rose yesterday
higher than ever known before by the Oldest
fnhabitant. All day parts Of the city were sub
merged Toward evening the waters began to
recede. and this morning the city had resumed
something of it, usual aspect, the streets that
were flooded yesterday being covered with ooze

al! the wharves and streets along the river front
were under water while the Potomac, turbid
and swollen and stretching far over its banks,
was rushing ON. bearing on its surface the
debris that told of the destruction wrought
along its course. The waters continued to rise
Saturday night, and by midnight the levels in
the center Of the city south of Pennsylvania
avenue began to overflow. Meanwhile, along
the river banks the scenes were grand and fright
full. Throngs of people were gathered at every
point, some engaged in the work Of saving
property, others looking upon the exciting
scene. The spectators were rewarded by many
thrilling sights. Early in the evening the
AnalOstan boat house was swept from its
foundations and carried down the torrent with
all its contents going finally to ruin against the
Long bridge. A schooner that was torn from
its anchorage in the Georgetown channel went
whirling down the stream, its bell tolling as it
swept along helplessly on its perilous voyage.
1t stranded near the monument. The wreckage
borne on the swift current was hurled and
heaped against the causeway and draw Of the
Long bridge. South of the bridge the wharves
and streets were flooded. The Eastern branch
spread far out beyond its accustomed bounds,
flooding the lower part of the hayward, over
flowing the Anacostia bridge. the causeway of
which was washed away, and inundating houses
on the low grounds. The arsenal point was
partly under water and part of the barracks
was cut off from the rest by a new branch of
the Potomac, which took its course across the
grounds.

Sunday morning the streets we're early

center of the city to see the unusual sight of
a city partly under water. Pennsylvania ave-
nue. was flooded from I'd street to 9TH street
west, and also in the neighborhood Of 9th street.
All the streets leading south from the Avenue,
between the Botanical Gardens and the Treas
ury were canals. The Easements and lower
floors Of houses were under water. The mar
ket-house stood in the center of a great lake.
The waters rose up nearly to the top step of
the Baltimore and Potomac depot. and the
trucks OF the RAILROAD cars about the station
were under water. On some parts of Pennsyl-
yanla avenue the water rose nearly to the floor
OF the street cars, which continued to run.
Nenturesome persons IN carriages and wagons
drove through water hub deep and shared the
thoroughfare with wading bows. men on RATS
and gondolas improvised from boards which
their owners poled along. Boats also appeared
on the streets.

Pennsylvania avenue to point 200 or 300 yards
south of the market-house that the cars could
not go through. The water was foot above
the floor of the cars Enterprising owners of
buses, with high bodies. established tempo
rary transportation lines, and did good bust
ness ferrying or fording persons over at 10

ing scenes about the streets. Along
the river front, wherever there were

was the Aqueduct bridge. All the dav the
streets leading to the bridge were crowded
with vehicles and pedestrians. The cars on
the Metropolitan and Washington and George

every available inch of space being occupied,

and swlrllng against the steep hillside streets
leading up from the river 'front.' Hundreds
continued their journey farther up to witness
the grand sights at the Chain bridge and the
Little Falls. where the river rushed with a
mighty roar IN its pent-up channel, overflow
Ing the bridge and sweeping great trees and
wrecks of barns and houses along in its re-

In almost every great disaster among the
steamboats, of the Mississippi river some ideal
Bludsoe or realistic Given has appeared to
leave the impress of his heroism and self-sac-
rifice upon the terrible event Charity Lam
bert, the simple black negress whose bravery
saved SO many lives in the recent explosion of
the Corona, is one of these heroic souls.
Charity was born in Maryland--when she does
not know. The browning glory of her life was
her heroism in this disaster, in which forty
souls were hurled into eternity without warn
ing. Charity was taken aboard the boat by
Capt. Blanks as chambermaid The Inflated
boat was ascending the river at the usual rate
of speed and Charity Was toward the rear of
the boat ironing when she heard the whistle
blow.


The familiar footing of the Corona had
scarcely died away when the most terrific ex-
plosion that ever shocked her ears took place
and the gallant craft sbIvered and shook and
seemed TO be parting in two. Nanny had
scarcely time to look around when the door
burst open and the ladies ran in Imploring her
assistance. Her quick intuition came 10 her
aid and she saw that something must be done
and done quickly to save the passengers Hur-
riedly. but calmly, she went to the place where
the life preservers were kept and parceied theta
out to the terror-stricken ladies until all were
supplied but herself, aud. needless Of her own
safety, she led the way to the roof


All who had been provided with life preserv-
ers by the noble. sef-sacrifcing old negress
hoated on the surface and were saved, except
Mrs. Hough, who was struck by door aud
drowned beneath the weight above her head
Old Nanny, after struggling in the water for
several minutes was finally rescued by roust-
about. Ever unseltish, she begged her rescuer
to save the white ladies first and leave her to
take care of herself

text:
Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALD.
New York, September 7.-One of the
most determined attempts at suicide ever
heard OF was made last night by Lena
Hertzog, II years of age, who resides
with her parents in Williamsburg. She
was passenger on ferryboat from
Brooklyn on the 1910 O'Clock trip last
night to this city. When the boat
reached Grand street ferry on this side,
Miss Hertzog came ashore, but immedi-
ately returned and paid her fare, and
once more took a seat in the cabin.
The boat had just cleared the
slip when she walked rapidly out of
the cabin and jumped overheard. The
boat was stopped and life preservers,
ladders and ropes were called into requi.
sition. The electric light made things as
clear as day. The first life preserver
thrown fell close to the girl, but she
pushed it away with an angry gesture.
The noise and shouts attracted Ticket
taker James Kelly, who has already
saved fourteen persons from drown
ing. He jumped into the river, seized
the girl by the waist and lifted her
bodily up so that she could breathe. The
girl turned upon him and struggled to
free herself from his grasp. Kelly: held
on, however, aud made for the slip. A
desperate struggle followed. The half.
drowned girl seemed to gain strength
and fought like tigress. When near
the slip ropes were thrown out. Kelly
caught one and wound it around the
body of his charge, but it was
quickly thrown off. This the girl
repeated three times and then
Selling her rescuer by the arm, savageiy
bit him. Kelly was becoming exhausted
and saw that if the girl was to be saved,
violence would have to be used, SO he
was compelled to beat her into submits
sion. The blows had the desired effect
for time, but when an attempt was
made to lit her up on the ladder,
she broke out afresh, but was
finally landed wet, limp and exhausted.
This water battle lasted fully fifteen
minutes. When stimulants were offered
the girl later on, she threw the glass
from her and smashed it. Finally the
reckless creature was placed under
arrest and afterwards sent to the
hospital in an ambulance, where today
she was doing nicely. Her parents say
the whole adventure arose from love
affair.

Three Druses, an isolated and peculiar sect
who have lived for generations near Mount
Lebanon, were among q lot Of Syrians landed
at Castle Garden Saturday. They were fine
looking, intelligent men. Two were farmers
and the third shoe maker. They left the
garden for Baltimore. The number Of the race
is set at 40, 000 They claim Hakem, the third
Fatimite Caliph, as their founder and paw him
divine honors. These people are divided into
two classes-the elect and the ignorant. The
elect are the high priests and the ignorant are
those who are too young and inexperienced TO
be initiated into the mysteries Of their religion
The high priests guard the mysteries of their
faith zealously, and tolerate neither Hebrew
nor Christians. The ignorant are far less con-
servative and frequently mingle socially with
believers in their creeds. The elect Druses be-
lieve that Jesus Christ was merely an ordinary
prophet and that Hakem was really God, mani
Tested in the flesh. They. are CONFIDENT. too.
that the number Of orthodox Druses can never
decrease or increase.

Benjamin G. Lum, bookkeeper at the New
Haven savings bank, was accidently locked up
in the bank vault Friday afternoon, and his
whereabouts was mystery until the vault was
opened for business Saturday morning at 9
O'Clock. Just before closing the bank Friday
Bookkeeper Lum carried his books into the
vault and while arranging them struck his head
III some way against ~ shelf with such force as
to render him unconscious. Shortly after
Treasurer ]. T. Tuttle. supposing that Lum
had gone home, closed the vault and set the
time lock. During the night Lum's family
grew anxious over his unusual absence and
early Saturday morning began searching for
him. No trace could be found and the bank
officials finally concluded that he must have
been locked up in the safe. The party reached
the bank just at opening hours. and when
Treasurer Iuttle hurriedly opened the door Lum
hastily stepped out where he could get breath
OF air. decidedly hungry, but none the worse
for his fifteen hours close confinement In
answer to inquiries, Lum said:


Il feel trst-rate and am as bright as a dollar
but | was anxiously awaiting the opening of
that big door. Yesterday when | was putting
up the books my head felt as if some one had
struck me, and lost consciousness When
recovered the vault was dark and I realized
that had been locked in. l Immediately felt
a round and found the candles and matches
and lighting them made myself as comfortable
as possible and had nothing to do but wait
patiently for morning.

A special from Lafayette Ind, records a

colored men approached the house and asked
Mrs. Smith to give them something to eat. On
being refused they went into the house and,
learning that there was no one at home but
Mrs. Smith and her little babe, forced her into
the yard and began ransacking the house.
After appropriatng all that they could find in
the way of money and valuables they set fire to
the house and added horrors to the terrible
scene by forcing the distracted woman to wit
ness the most brutal Of fiendish deeds, which
was the tossing of her little baby in the air and
letting it fall back almost on the point Of sharp
knives which they held under it. The brutes
finally needed the frantic womans entreaties
and went away, leaving her with nothing to
greet the return of her horrOr-stricken husband
and children but her half-dead babe and
smouldering heap of Goals where was, only a
few hours before, their home. People for
miles around have been searching the country
for the villains and at last accounts three of
the men had been captured.

LONDON, Sept. 10.-At $50 this morning Q
policeman found the body Of an abandoned
woman lying in a corner Of a railway arch
spanning Cable street, in Whitechapel Exam
ination Of the body showed that the head and
legs had been cut off and carried away and the
stomach ripped open, leaving the bowels lying
upon the ground. The police authorities
Immediately placed a Gordon of officers around
the spot, but no arrests were made. A police.
man passed the place where the body was found
every fifteen minutes throughout the night and
saw nothing to arouse his suspicious.


THE medical EXAMINATION.


Physicians who examined the body believe
that the murder occupied nearly an hour and
it is surmised that the murderer carried the
head and legs away in q bag. The murder Ia
the most horrible of the whole Whitechapel
series. The dissection of the body showed that
the perpetrator possessed considerable surgical
skill The murdered woman was about thirty
years Of age and was evidently addicted to ex-
cessive use OF spirituous liquors. Her clothing
was shabby. As yet she has not been identi-
fed The murder has created tremendous ex-
element and large crowd Of agitated human
ity surrounds the morgue, whittier the body
was taken.


SUPPOSED TO HAVE BEEN KILLED TWO DAYS AGO.


Further examination reveals the fact that
there was no blood on the ground where the
body was found, nor were there any indications
of a struggle. This confirms the general belief
that the woman was murdered in a house and
her body taken to the spot where it was discov-
cred. The trunk was nude and q torn and
bloody chemise was lying near it. Experts
are Of the opinion that the woman was killed
two days ago.

DENVER, Colo, November 9.-The
Republicans Trinidad special says: The
bodies of John Martin and Henry Miller,
the cowboys who were frozen to death
near Sierra Grande, last week during
the blizzard, were brought to Folsom for
burial. Their two companions, Charlie
Wier and Henry Jolly, were taken to
Ration for medical treatment. Jolly will
lose all his fingers, but otherwise will
not suffer greatly. Wier will lose all
his fingers, and one Of his feet is
horribly frozen. -Four other men
belonging to the same party are missing
and it is feared they are dead. Their
names are Charlie Rand, Mama, Ed.
Jaeger, Joe Evans, and two Mexicans,
names unknown. 1t is reported by par
ties who know that at least twenty men
are missing from their homes, and it is
feared that many of them will be found
dead.


jolly and Weir tell a heart.rending
story Of their sufferings. They say the
blizzard struck them Wednesday night
OF last week. They were holding q herd
of $500 cattle. The wind became
q hurricane before morning, and
when Martin and jolly Went to
the last guard about 8 a. m-, the storm
was 30 binding they could not hold the
herd. Jolly started to camp for help.
In the meantime Miller and Weir had
LETT the camp to assist holding the cattle.
jolly could not find the camp, and Miller
and Wier could not find the herd, All
three were drawn together by shouting,
and wandered around until dayliohf'
when they found Martin. The cold was
so bitter that the men entered an arroyo.
and, after fastening their horses, took
their saddle blankets and buried them
selves in snowdrifs. This was at about
: O'Clock in the afternoon, and by only
the greatest effort Wier and Jolly sue
ceeded in keeping awake. They were
slightly apart from Martin and Miller,
and had difficulty in talking to each
other. The snow piled upon them in
such immense weight that they were
compelled to seek another drift.


About O'Clock Friday morning Miller
called Jolly and Wier and told them they
had all better 60. And when they crawled
out they made search in the drift for
Miller and Martin. The latter only was
found, and he was dead. They took
their horses and started, leading them a
few rods. when they found Miller on his
knees with his bleeding face against the
blast, swaying to and fro, his horse
standing in front of him, as though
trying to protect him from the cold.
He YVES asked to get I'D and
go With them. He was unable to rise
and was assisted to his feet, but could
not walk. jolly started to get assistance
while Wier remained with their dying
companion. Both Wier's hands were
frozen and he was helpless to render any
help, and was fast becoming insensible
himself, when Mexican found him and
took him to Rhodes' ranch, a few miles

less.

First Experience In q Sleeping Car.


From the Chicago Herald


II see some queer things while knocking
around the country" said a travelling man yes
terday, "and one of the funniest circumstances
that can recall happened last Friday night I
was running up the Milwaukee road few hum
dred miles, and when left Sioux City my only
fellow passengers were an old man and his wife,
who occupied the lower section across from me.
They had their berth made up early and soon
retired. guess it was the first time they had
ever travelled in sleeper, by thu way they
acted, for they were pretty awkward about un-
dressing, and heard the old lady lecture her
husband for not getting larger room. After
much mutual grumbling all was quiet, and then
came deep snore, accompanied by one a trif1e
more subdued. 1t was evident the old people
were asleep. At Manila Junction a large party
came In and taxed the sleeper to its full
capacity. The porter had to remove the bag
gage OF the couple, which was slowed above
them, and assigned the berth to a little, inof-
fensive citizen weighing about 100 pounds. He
removed his shoes and was climbing into the
bunk when the old lady woke up and began
screaming. This aroused her husband and he
yelled for the porter, who came runni ing down
the aisle. Say, there's man Just come into
our room,' the old gentleman gasped out. The
porter tried to explain that he would not annoy
them and had right to be there. But neither
would believe this and the old man declared
that the porter had let him in to rob them.
He was also indignant to think any one should
be allowed to sleep in the same compartment
as his wife, and finally he and the old lady got
up and dressed and insisted on the porter re-
moving the bedding from their berth, SO they
could use the seats. 1 peeped through the
curtains and saw them both sitting there nod
ding, but every few minutes they would sud-
denly remember and sit bolt upright. pitied
the poor, deluded couple, and really the situa-
ton was not lacking in pathos, for they were
thoroughly in earnest. When I got off the
train early next morning they were still sitting
there, but both were sound asleep, the old
gentleman with his arms around his wife's
waist and her head pillowed on his shoulder"

There is now in progress at Parkersburg, W.
Va, trial Of seventeen-year-old girl named
Eta Robinson, whose life has for the past six
months been full of sensations. The charge
against her is horse stealing, and the circum-
stances attending the committing Of the crime
are romantic. Six months ago Eta was visit
ing her brother, who resides in the adjoining
county Of Putnam and is engaged as farm
hand by Thomas Handley, real estate owner.
One morning Eta was missing, and also fine
horse belonging to Nathan Mccoy.


After search of some days throughout the
neighborhood, including some Of the toughest
OF West Virginia hills and thicket ravines, the
horse was found in the girls possession near
the Ohio river. While her pursuers were
debating what to do with her Eta dashed into
the Ohio, still on horseback. and endeayored to
swim across. She was captured and placed in
jail, but broke out and returned to her brother,
when Mccoy, from whom she had stolen the
horse. took pity on her youth and refused to
prosecute her.


A short time after horse belonging to a
farmer named Smith was missing, Just at the
time when the low country in the Kanawha
valley was all flooded The horse was tracked
to the edge Of the waters. The next day both
Eta and the horse were found in hollow.
The girl had swan the stream, a mile wide, on
norsepack. she slept out at night, living on
what she could steal For the second time her
youth protected her and she was not prose-
cuted. Six weeks later she stole a horse from
Lewis Lesley. She was pursued across ths
Ohio, captured and brought back to the Put
nam county Jail She was confined there sew
eral weeks, in which time her winning ways
won her entrance into the confidence of the
jailer, who allowed her many privileges.


Two weeks ago he awoke to find the fair
maid gone, she having cleverly made her escape
by cutting through an old wall. It was after
ward found that she had stolen suit of mems
clothes and fine horse temporarily in the
jailers possession and fed the country. She
was finally captured, with the horse still
In her possession near her old home. During
her escapades, she had lived on berries, corn
or anything she could find, and alone wandered
through the widest and most danseroust erri-
tory.


This young adventures does not steal from
any other motive than simply the love Of ex-
element and adventure. Her face glows with
youth and apparent innocence, and her every
look and action deny that her peculiar conduct
is from evil motives. Her beauty and general
excellence in many ways have created vast
deal OF sympathy in her favor. The trial will
probably last week,

SAN Francisco, March 19-The glove
contest between Jimmie Carroll, for
merly of Boston, and Sam Blakelock, OF
England, took place to. night in the rooms
of the California Athletic Club. The
men weighed 1873 pounds each. Young
Mitchell and George Mcdonald were
Blakelock's seconds, and Sam Fitzpat :
rick and Tom Meadows acted for Carroll
Hiram Cook was chosen referee. Fifteen
hundred people were present. Time was
called at 8 AS.


In the first two rounds the men
spared cautiously. Blakelock led, but
Carroll avoided him. In the third round
Blakelock got in a sharp one on Carroll's
mouth with his left, and in the fifth Car
roll got in heavy blow on Blakelock's
nose, drawing first blood. Fierce fight
ing followed. Carroll doing the best
work. From the sixth to the tenth
round considerable rushing was done,
the honors being apparently even. In
the tenth round Carroll got in a terrific
right handler, knocking Blakelock down.
In the eleventh round Carr oil scored an
other knockdown, but the rushing pace
told, and both men appeared weak.
In the twelfth Blakelock came up fresh,
but Carroll rushed him around the ring,
bent on finishing him up. Sammy took
his punishment bravely, showing consid-
cradle cleverness. The thirteenth round
opened with Blakelock groggy but plucky
Carroll got in a number of vicious upper
cuts. Blakelock tapping him feebly
In the fourteenth Blakelock got in
several good stabs with his left,
and in the fifteenth led low, where
upon Carroll claimed foul, which was
not gallowed. Carroll then rushed his
opponent, the latter clinching in the
effort to save himself. Carroll whirled
around, hitting the Englishman in the
face, but the latter would not 60 down.
In the sixteenth round Carroll started in
with rush, giving blow after
blow. Blakelock struggled man
fully to hold his own, but
Carroll was too strong for him, and
finished his work with terrific right
handler, laying the Englishman senseless.


The fight WAS one of the pluckiest ever
seen in. the city. Both men displayed
about equal science. Carroll's superior
strengths, however, proved too much for
Blakelock, and won him the fight.

CHICAGO, January 21.-A ten-round fight
between Mike Barrett. of Peoria. and Dan.
Washburn, of Elgin, attracted large crowd of
sports to the town of jefferson YESTERDAY.
Washburn tried rushing from the first, and re-
ceived severe punishment. Barrett clearly
had the best of the fight from the second
round. In the eighth round Washburn's face
was SO badly swollen and cut that his features
were hardly recognizable. Barretts left eye
was closed. but he showed no other signs of
punishment. The men had been together but
moment in the tenth round when Barretts
right suddenly shot out and landed with crush
ing effect on Washburn's neck. The youngster
went down like log and lay on the floor for
fifteen seconds. The fight and the money were
then given to Barrett

rounding property was very great. Small

The crowds of people making for Oklahoma
every day grows larger and larger at Kansas
City, where the big union depot cannot ac-
commodate those who pass through. Fully
500 boomers outfits passed through Yelling
ton, Kan, yesterday. At Arkansas City the an
nouncement of Captain Hayes, who is CON-
handing the cavalry detailed to guard the
border there, that settlers would be allowed to
cross the line into the Cherokee strip imme-
diately after midnight Thursday, has created a
great stir among the prospectors, and it is
thought that the large majority of them will
take advantage Of the opportunity, and that
midnight tonight will witness grand rush
into the strip. The campers realize that all
cannot cross the border at the same place, and
there will be scampering along the border
for miles. A terrible wind and rain-storm
passed over Arkansas City Wednesday night
which played sal havoc with the boomers
tents. Women and children were drenched
and badly frightened
