From Flag to Flag"


Suddenly all was furry and excitement to
prepare for the cyclone that even the very liz
yards knew was coming. Sledge-hammers,
axes, and immense timbers were hastily
brought inside the house. We rapidly pre-
pared to occupy and defend the three front
rooms only. Ciriaco brought in some cold
meat and bread, brandy, aqaadie'te, and pail
of water, which were deposited in a corner of
the parlor.


The rear of the house (Which was one story
in height, with walls 8 feet thick, built of
stone and cement, and with immense beams of
solid cedar sustaining the stone roof was
closely barred and secured in the strongest way
possible, There was sudden and hurried rush
into the various buildings. Chinese and me-
groes fed to their respective barracoons and
fastened themselves in. Lamo. with two white
men in our employ, and several trusty, stall
wart negroes. waited to see that all were pro-
tected, thoroughly safe as possible, barely al
lowing themselves time to rush into the house
and close the last windows. when the hurricane
broke upon US. The wind rose in great, howl
ing gusts, and swooped down and around with
tumultuous roar like the booming of cannon.
A rattle and bang. as though we were being
assaulted with batteringrams on one side the
house. and all rushed to the threatened
windows TO secure them with great solid tim
bers driven by sledge-hammers into the pol
ished floor, and forced against the massive
panels of the shutters that closed within.
rushing and a whiZzing sound. broken
into prolonged roar, admonished US that
the wind had veered, and now the opposite
windows were threatened; before they could
be properly secured, great rafting and
bowling at the door drove every one with axes.
sledge-hammers and timbers to the front of
the house. So the wind whirled round and
round. stopping at every door and window to
blow louder and more startling blast Like a
great giant battling for admission, or a beseig-
ing army attacking first on one side, then on
another, then all around at once, in the deter
mination to carry the defenses by storm. the
merciless wind fought. We knew only too well
that if it gained admission. the house would be
wrecked; one of its mighty blasts could lift the
very stone roof.


Meanwhile. except for a single candle in
corner, so shielded for fear OF sudden gusts
that it only served to make darkness visible, we
were without any light. panel a few inches
square. hung on hinges in a front shutter. was
our only means of obtaining glimpse of the
outside world, and We dared not open this
while the storm was doing its utmost. For
thirty hours we bravely and increasingly de-
Tended the besieged castle thirty hours of NOR
tai terror and incessant vigilance-before the
giant with one last. deafening howl, dimin-
ished the force of the attack. and gave us one
moments peace. Cautiously taking hurried
peeps through the little panel, while the tor
nado was whirling with fearful impetuosity
through roseate atmosphere, the very wind
seemed a tangible pink element sweeping
everything before it. Debris of every kind was
being borne upon its mighty wings. Great
sheets of metal roofing from the sugar-house
went careering along like scraps of paper;
huge palm trees whirled aloft and away like
straws. while tiles. bricks. and smaller objects
sailed with lightning rapiditv across the horizon
like notes in breeze, utterly insignificant
were they in the grasp of the mighty element
4 few holes. wrenched through the strong stone
roof of the house, gave access to the rain that
now poured down in binding floods. and we
were soon like Noah's dove-flying in vain
search of dry spot.


When at last, after thirty hours of exhaus-
tive battle and mortal alarm, our doors were
once more thrown open, the scene of desolation
was beyond all powers of description. The
bourrdless fields of waving cane, that delighted
our dyes only two days before, had entirely dis
appeared: beaten fiat down by the wind, the
rapidly descending waters rushed completely
over them. The sugar-house was wholly I'M
rooted; and for DAYS broad strips of the metal
bent as though Vulcan's hammer had beaten
them into a thousand fantastic shapes. were
brought from the fields hundreds of yards
away. Rock fences had been dashed to pieces
and the fragments strewed over the fields. The
proud army of majestic palms. that had for so
many decades stood guard of our entrance, lost
twenty of its bravest veterans. Desolation was
everywhere SuDremel

districts in the centred valleys and on the At
lantic coast, except in southeast New England

merous showers are reported The weather
for the week was unfavorable for small grains
in Minnesota and Dakota, owing to the small

ported. Wheat harvestFs in progress in GEN.

week. A short crop Of timothy and clover is

sive rains interrupted cultivation and harvest
work. Crops were generally retarded in Ken
lucky and Tennessee owing to heavy daily
rains and little sunshine. Reports from North
Carolina, South Carolina. Alabama and Lousi-
ana indicate that the weather was favorable
for all crops, which show decided improvement
since the recent rains. In Mississippi and

have been more or less injured. The excessive

New BEDFORD, Mass. September 90
The report of Lieutenant. Commander
Stockton, of the United States steamer
Thetis, to the Navy Department concern
ing the loss of the little bark Ohio, of this
port, in the Arctic ocean, encloses letter
from John Kelly, an employee at Hope,
on the American coast, Arctic ocean,
which gives facts never before made
public. The letter states that October
opened with fresh northeast wind the


ground had frozen, The temperature
ranged from ten to twenty-five degrees,
and the land was white with snow.
just before the blizzard began the
Ohio was off Cape Lisburne, land
being plainly in sight. Two
banks were near and hove to. Massive


rollers struck the vessel with great vio-


lence, lifting her up and throwing her
closer in, the spray leaping clear over
the lower yards. Captain Allen had
ordered the mast cut away, but man


could not stand anywhere without hold
ing with one or both hands. A few men


went up the main mast and several up the


mizzen. Many sought shelter about the


cabin tops and between the galley and
cabin entrance. The house fell in,
trapping the men underneath, and then


the ship broke in three parts about
the mizzen and just abaft the tryworks,


and except for part of the bow, the Ohio


disappeared. Thirteen men were carried


ashore by the waves, through flying de-


bris, and three men came down on dry


land from the mainmast when it went


over. The men sought shelter with the
natives, who agreed to care for them I'M
til ship would take them off. Two flags
were set to attract the attention Of pass
ing ships. Captain Bayne, at the whal-
ing station, let the men have q
whale boat and all the clothing
and blankets he had. Ship after
ship passed without noticing the colors.
On October 18th the steamer Belvidere
passed twelve miles out. Seven men
took the whaleboat and tried to intercept
her, and were never heard of again,


their boat probably being swamped.


Late in the evening the steamer
Narwhal, Captain McGregor, came
along, saw the flag, luffed up
under the point, waited q little


while and then kept off. If the whale
boat had not been gone the men could
have saved themselves. Captain Bayne
moved his stores outside and took the


men into the station, and clothed and
fed them as we'll as his resources would
permit. Six of the men were taken
away on the William Lewis in July, and
three others were taken by the United

Saturdays game Of ball between Washington
and Boston was an exciting struggle, twelve in
nings in length. without a conclusion. The
score stood to 4. when the darkness became
TOO intense to allow the game to proceed, and
Umpire Powers whose decisions had been
favored up to that point with a Bostonese
aroma suddenly became imbued with pity for
the struggling Senators and called the game.
The contest was close and exciting, and after
the first two innings, which were disgrace to
the home team, were played the fielding was
beautiful and brilliant. The Washington bats
men hit the ball hard hit it and often, but they
could not hit together, except in two spots, and
although they outbatted the visitors they were
seriously handicapped by the lead which the
Bostonians made early IN the game on poor
field work. Beecher, Wise and Wilmot led the
batting Wilmot made a single and triple,
Beecher two doubles, and Wise single and
double.


THE RUNS


Haddock and DAILY ard GARRISON, CAMEL and
Kelly were the batteries. The visitors made
couple Of runs in the first one on Richardson's
drive over the fence and the other on Kelly's
base on balls. Days wild throw to second and
Rows high throw home. in the second the
guests increased their lead one point on
Beecher's muff, Wise's fumbling and Mack's
throw to the stand to catch a runner. Then
the game logged along evenly without man
touching the plate until the sixth. when sim
giles by Brother John and Hoy, triple to the
right fence by Wilmot and a scratch double by
Wise gave the home team three runs, tying
the score. This condition did not last the
inning through. however. for Johnston scored
on his double hit and fnmbles by Brother John
and Wise. The eighth saw the home team pull
up even again. scoring on Beecher's two-base
drive, Wise's single and Kelly's bad throw
home.


The game was called at the end Of the
twelfth. after lasting two hours and twenty-five
minutes. Washington made IL hits and 8
errors and Boston 10 hits and errors.

BALTIMORE, Sept. 24.-The hog cholera in
Kent county is rapidly spreading and unless
some active step is taken by the authorities the
disease will create untold havoc among the
swine in southern Maryland. Kent county has
suffered heavily; about two hundred hogs have
just been lost and more will surely follow.
Farmers are seriously to blame for much of
this trouble, because they persist in throwing
the dead carcasses into the woods or streams.
The losses aggregate a fairly astounding
amount of money every year. Two officers left
last night for Queen Anne's county town
(Centeryille) to inform themselves about two
serious outbreaks there. This county has
been visited by this disease at frequent inter-
walls, although free from bovine pleuro.

TEMPTING PREPARATIONS FOR THE TABLE.
One of the daintiest and prettiest of table
dishes to which it contributes is the orange
basket. For this choose handsome thin skinned
oranges; cut them in two, being careful to cut
evenly, take out the pulp, and separate each
section, removing the seed. but break the in
side skin as little as possible. Throw the peel
into cold water an hour or two to stiffen. Now
take some fine wire and make handle to each
outside half thus forming the baskets; twist
bit of orange-colored ribbon around each
handle, and fill the baskets with the orange Sec
tons nicely sugared or jellies arrange on a
dish with few sprigs of orange leaves, or
something resembling them which can always
be procured at florists. and you have q very
effective and not a common dish.


FILLING ORANGES WITH JELLY


is another way Of preparing a delicious dish.
The method of doing this is to cut small.
round piece of the skin from the stem end.
then with the finger loosen the pulp from the
skin and gradually work the finger between the
skin and pulp until il is entirely loosened. Then
draw the pulp out through the opening without
breaking the skin. Throw the skins into cold
water until wanted. Have ready an orange or
wine jelly. drain the orange skins. fill them
with the jelly, and stand away to cool When
cold cut them into halves and then into quar-
tiers. and arrange them on a pretty DISH gar
nlshed with smilax.

sugar lemon juice and pulp. Cut the oranges

boiling corn starch over them and stand away

Last night about 9 O'Clock a young
woman named Mrs. Henney attempted
to commit suicide on Main street, near
Washington. At.hat hour Mrs. Henney
went into drugstore and asked for some
laudanum. In accordance with the law,
the druggist asked the woman what the
laudanum was for. She snatched the
bottle containing the fluid out of his
hand, and told him it didn't make any
difference, she had the bottle. Then she
said she wanted it for a sick friend, and
walked out, meeting young man on the
sidewalk. The two talked for few Sec
onds, and then she put the bottle to her
mouth and started to drink its contents.
The young man snatched it away from
her, but not soon enough to prevent her
from swallowing some of it's
contents. A few minutes later
she was taken with convulsions,
and was carried into a fruitstand
and the patrol wagon was called. Medi-
cal aid arrived before the patrol wagon,
and she was relieved of the drug and
taken to her home on Pine street. She
said her husband was in the northern
part of the State, but refused to give any
reason for her act.

DULUTH, April 20.-As train of four
teen loaded cars, with Superintendent
Hopes private car attached was descend
ing heavy grade between Two Harbors
and Yakadina, on the Duluth and Iron
Range Railroad, the air brakes refused to
work, and the train gained frightful ve-
locity. The brakeman managed to un-
couple the private car, which was soon
stopped by the hand brakes. The rest OF
the train plunged madly on, reaching a
speed of 110 miles per hour, and finally
left the track, demolishing the engine
and all the cars. Engineer Charles
Cutler had both legs broken. Two other
men were seriously hurt.

READING. JAN 10.-There is mourning and
sorrow in many households in Reading to-day.
Over one hundred spirits are hushed forever
in death as the result of the wreck and ruin
wrought in this city by the storm of last night.
The cyclone left the entire city in darkness,
which was only relieved by the electric lights
and huge bonfires which shed their lurid glare
on the scene of death. All night long brave
and willing hands assisted in the work of the
rescue of the dead The disaster is fully as
Dad as reported in these dispatches last night


OVER HUNDRED PERIsHED.


The list of fatal cases will fully reach one
hundred and may be more. The hospitals and
undertakers' establishments are filled with the
victims. The physicians all busy and many
private houses have been opened for the ac-
commodation of the injured. The ruined silk
mill presents scene of desolation. The Polish
church disaster. several months ago, was one
of the most horrible accidents that had startled
the community. but ii sinks into comparative
insignificance when placed in parallel with the
awful visitation of last evening. Mayor Kenney
at O'Clock this morning issued the following
proclamation:


II earnestly appeal to the professional
business, and other citizens who may be
able to favorably respond, to meet at the
court house this afternoon at l:30 to devise
ways and means to aid the injured and assist
the families of those who persisted last night
in the fall of the silk mill and at the Philadel-
phla and Reading railroad paint shop. The
fearful cyclone that struck this city at 80 last
evening has brought sorrow and want to many
OF our people who are in such circumstances as
m hn h1a 20
occason calls loudly for immediate action.
Quick to respond to others in distress, let us
not fall to do speedy justice to our own grief
stricken people,"


THE WORK OF RESCUE RETARDED.


The work of rescue was greatly retarded
from the singular manner in which the silk
mill collapsed. 1t did not blow over, as might
have been expected from the terrible force of
the wind, but was bodily crushed down, falling
IN upon itself in one mass, not a vestige of the
walls remaining standing above the stone
foundation. The rafters and timbers of the
flooring projected in all directions As the
building was steam-heated. fortunately the
ruins did not take fire, otherwise not one of
the unfortunates could possibly have escaped
death In Its most appalling form.


THE ONLY EYEWITNESS TO THE DISASTER,
80 far as is known, was a Mrs. GemmiI. resid-
ing at 1150 Mulberry street. AT about twenty
minutes of O'Clock, !" said she to reporter, II
heard an awful crash. and thinking it was a
new house which is being put up alongside of
us, ran to the front door. A great cloud of
dust hung over the silk mill. and could hear
the crashing of timbers and the roar of the
falling walls. The next moment / saw the
whole mill a great heap of ruins, from the
midst of which came such awful moaning and
groaning and terrible cries as 1 never want to
hear again. Not soul did L see come out of
the mill, and it seemed many minutes to me
before anybody came to the spot / stood
there in the door like one struck dumb until
my husband came running from his work"
Teams of every description, omnibuses. fu-
neral coaches, fre-wagons, hospital vans and
private vehicles were pressed into service and
were running rapidly to and from the scene of
the disaster all night long, bearing the bodies
of the wounded, dying and dead to their homes
or to the different hospitals.


DOWN TO DEATH WITHOUT WARNING.
From the statements of some of those who
escaped from the building il appears to have
gone down in an instant. There was a loud
crash of breaking timber, and the persons in
the mill all rushed toward the main doors
good many OF them succeeded in getting out
while four girls saved themselves by jumping
from the second-story windows. The first
rumbling noise followed instantly by the
falling OF the building, the upper stories going
first with their human load. Had it not been
for the fact that but few of the hands were on
the third and fourth floors at the time scarcely
life would have been saved. Mr. Geo. Grim
shaw, one of the proprietors of the mill. who
was in the Office at the time and barely escaped
with his life, having received several severe
wounds on the head, stated that there were to
the best Of his knowledge about 275 persons.
principally girls and boys, in the establish
ment at the time of the occurrence. Up to 8
O'Clock this morning the large majority of the
victims were still in the ruins.

DARING FEAT OF A BEAUTY OF THE FOOTHILLS
From the Chico Enterprise.


Near Forest Ranch, in the mountains above
Chico, resides young lady who for grit and
pluck we'll take off our hat to every time.
The lady in question Miss Kate Lucas. resides
on mountain ranch with her mother and
brothers, the latter being engaged in furnish
ing the meat used by the large lumber crews
high up in the Sierras. Miss Lucas is tall.
1.-the and well-built girl, with red, rosy cheeks.
jet black hair, bright, flashing eyes, and is
the acknowledged belle of that vicinity.
She is an intrepid horsewoman, and
rides fearlessly and alone over the noun
tain slopes and through the -ravines. She
scorns saddle and at times rides fiery mus
taug without either bride or blanket, simply
using iariat, the end tied around her horse 5
head and neck. She is a capital shot with the
rifle and has worsted many Of the crack shots
there by her unerring aim. She has been out
with her brothers hunting, and very rarely fails
to bag deer or other wild animals which SO
abound in that section. Sometimes the young
miss assists IN capturing the wild cattle when
they are required for the market. and then the
lariat Is twirled with precision that often puts
the vaqueros to shame.


A few weeks ago, after daring ride after n
particularly wild and feet-footed steer. which
showed tight from the start, the young lady
laughed at the vaquero, who seemed afraid of
the animal, and smilingly challenged him to
.nfo" rope over the anlmals head and ride
him. The vaquero declined with thanks. Miss
Lucas then displayed piece of courage and
daring worthy of the ancient Roman arena
Springing from her horse, she went up to the
bound and believing beast. quickly and
deftly tied rope around his head and
neck, then told the vaquero to let him
loose. This he did reluctantly. and the en-
ragged steer was quickly Oh its feet but equally
as quick the fearless lass was on its back. Then
commenced a ride that is rarely witnessed. For
half an hour the wild chase and ride was con-
tinued-over hill and dale, through brush and
canyon-when the steer gave completely out
and the triumphant girl led her captive to the
house. 1t was bold feat and the daring rider
has made herself famous in that section of the
country

New York, March 1.-THE steamer
Caroline Miller arrived last night with
news from Cape Haytien. Captain Mil
Ter said that twelve of Legitime's soldiers
who had been taken prisoners by Hyp-
polyte, were shot in the public square at
Cape Haytien the day before the steamer
left. Sympathizers with Legitime had
endeavored to get the men released and
Hyppolyte had become distrustful of
many of his officers. He, therefore, had
them put to death. Captain Miller said
that Cape Haytien was filled with
Legitime's spies. According to one of
the officers of the steamer, transport
was permanently engaged carrying arms
and other implements of war from Monte
Christie to Cape Haytien, for the use of
Hyppolite's men. The United States
steamer Galena was anchored at Cape
Haytien when the Miller left.

Notwithstanding the unpromising
aspect of the weather, there was good
attendance at the Agricultural Park yes
terday. the sports of both sexes being
present in large numbers to witness the
match race for $500 between the Misses
Myrtie Peek and Lizzie Williams.


Owing probably to report having
been spread that the latter lady was
only local amateur, the race was talked
of beforehand as foregone conclusion,
and that this opinion was universal was
shown by the mum bers who backed her
opponent at odds of two to one. The
sequel proved however that she is in no
particular behind the so-called "cham-
ion," Miss Peek, unless it be on the
score of experience. The track was in
first-class condition and as consequence,
the time was, for such an
event, unusually fast. At O'Clock,
the time set for the first event,
Miss Peek, mounted on Mr.. Budinger's
promising colt Origin, ran mile against
the famous riderless horse Longview,
who, however, beat her by three lengths,
in :57. This being merely an exhibi-
tion race, but little interest was mani
tested in it, everybody being anxious for
the event of the day. However, after
wait of about twenty minutes, during
which brisk sale of pools at two to one
on Miss Peek was made, the fair eques-
triepnes appeared upon the track in
company with Mr.. Demorest, Miss
Peek's manager. The ladies, who were
attired respectively in black and blue
velvet habits, having tossed for choice
of horses, of which there were six, Miss
Peek won and chose alternately Ed.
Smith, Ghost and Origin, Miss Williams
taking Fandango, Athol and Hook Hook
ing. For some unknown reason the in
side track, which is ninety feet shorter
than the mile and good deal narrower
than the other track, was chosen as the
scene of the race, and the judges having
announced that the ladies would ride five
miles, changing horses at the end of
every mile, the ladies were led to the
post and got away to very good start.


Miss Williams having the inside track
At the half mile Miss Peek passed her
opponent and seemed to be gaining on
her, but, putting on spurt just before
entering the straight, Miss Williams
came in a good three lengths ahead, and
getting good start went away on her
second journey. In changing horses
Miss Peek was unfortunate, as her habit
catching in the horn of the saddle she
was thrown head downwards on the
wrong side of the horse. However,
through the combined efforts Of the
helper and her manager she regained her
seat and caught her opponent at the
three-quarter post, but again lost her
ground and came in three lengths be-
hind. Miss Williams getting off with
another good start led all the way round
the third mile and increased her lead by
some three lengths, but on changing for
the fourth mile Miss Peek got away in
fine style and led all the way to the
straight, and fine race home resulted
almost in dead heat. Changing for the
last time Miss Peek got away first; but
riding evidently ior ali she WAS worth,
Miss Williams caught her at the three
quarter post and passing her, came under
the wire fully four lengths ahead amid the
cheers of the excited throng. Time, 9:97

City, Utah, says: The sixtieth general semi

gan yesterday. Wilfred Woodruff. the
president Of the church, presided,

presidency was present There we're also pres

An Interesting Case Heard by JUS.


Iice Savage.


A most peculiar case, involving the
charge of using threatening and abusive
language, was heard in Justice Savage's
court yesterday morning. The COM
plainant was a Mrs. Jane Tremble, of
Burlington street, and the defendant was
Mrs. Mary Gully, of the same locality.
Previous to the hearing of the case Mrs..
Gully was brought up under arrest to an
swer to the charge Of non-appearance
last week when the case was set down for
trial, but after explanation to the Judge
she was released with reprimand. Sew
eral witnesses were examined, and one
of them testified that Mrs. Gully had
threatened to burn Mrs. Trem ble's house
down. Another witness testified that Mrs.
Gully had told Mrs. Tremble that her
teeth were false and her hair dyed. The
defendent denied the truth of the charges
and said she had been knocked down by
Mr.. Tremble and that her house had
been bombarded every night with scores
of oranges by the neighbors, that her
fences had been pulled down, that stones
and bottles had been thrown at her chill
dren by the neighbors, and that she and
her husband were in dread of their lives.
The defendant was represented by AL
leyne Orr, but the jury found her guilty
and she was ordered to appear for sem
tence on Monday morning.

entrance, where four guards were sta

bats and rocks, breaking in the windows

noisy that their whooping and shouting

streets, and caused wildly exaggerated
rumors to spread, which made the police

officers, to the scene. In less than three
fourths of an hour from the outbreak the
four ringleaders we're locked up in their
rooms, and everything was quiet. No

years ago.

SAN FRANcIscd, April 13,-John P.

lies on her side, completely out of water,

on shore, this vessel being completely
broken up. OF the Vandalia only the
main-mast, smoke-stack and some of

The German bark Peter Godeffroi, the

Trading Company, were driven ashore,

means was put to work on the Nipsic and

sprung and her propeller would not work.

shattered above the water line. All OF

Princeton Is Killed.


PRINCETON, Special Telegram, - A
fatal shooting affray occurred here late last
night. Policeman Norton was attempting
to arrest a young man named Joseph
Brumbaugh, who was drunk and raising
disturbance Oh the streets. Brumbaugh,
who is a powerful young fellow, resisted
the officer. The latter is small man, who
was severely wounded while in the army,
and was no match physically for Brum-
baugh. Norton yelled Justify for help
as Brumbaugh was dragging him
along the streets. Several citizens,
who heard the officers cries, were hurrylng
to his assitance when the shooting occurred
The officer broke loose from Brambaugh in
front of the Mile Laos County bank, when
the latter put his hand behind him as if to
draw weapon Norton drew his revolver and
fired, the shot taking effect in Brambaugh's
right breast passing diagonally through
his body, coming out under the left shoulder
blade. Brambaugh started to run and the
officer fired two more shots, each of which
took effect. Brambaugh ran about dozen
yards when he fell and expired instantly.
The inquest will be held tomorrow, and it
is the general opinion that the officer will
be justified.

HUME, Mo-, Special.-At Jackson cross
roads, six miles south of here burglars en-
tered the residence of Jasper James and de-
manded that he tell them where he had
hidden his savings. This he refused to do,
and failing to bring James to terms the
robbers attempted to terrorize his wife, but
were unsuccessful. Becoming convinced that
threats would not work the thieves tied the
husband and wife together, back to back.
Each in turn was pricked with pin and
burned about the head and face with
matches. Finally Mr.. James tainted from
the terrible torture to which he had been
subjected. His suffering wife, believing
that her husband was dead and
that her life would also be taken
unless she gave her assailants the
information sought. told the thieves where
$400 was concealed. The robbers secured
the booty, united their victims and de-
parted. Mrs. James labored for some time
to resuscitate her husband, and when she
had restored him to consciousness she fell
exhausted to the floor and died shortly aft
erwards. James is sixty-fv years old and
his wife was only two years younger.

Yesterday morning about $3.50 o'clock shoot
ing affray occurred at the front door of VIM.
Nlcholsons saloon, on Pennsylvania avenue,
between 18th and 18th streets, which came near
being tragedy. The shooting at such an early
hour in the morning caused some excitement
among the persons who don't go home till
mornin'." The report of the pistol was heard
by the officers several adjoining beats, and
all hastened in the direction of the sound, ex-
pecting to find the dead body of man and
possibly arrest n murderer. Policemen Ellis
and Heller were the first to arrive. VIM. Mich
olson, proprietor of the saloon, was there, and
he admitted having fired the shot John Shea,
who had received the bullet from the pistol in
the feshy part of the neck was also there
Both men were taken to the station. Nicholson
was held on charge of assault and battery
with intent to kill, and physician was sent for
to attend the injured man.


WHAT THE POLICE LEARNED.


The police investigated the shooting and say
they learned that Shea had caused the trouble;
that with companion named Hugh Flaherty
he had been in the saloon, and Shea had made
some trouble and was elected: that he went
away, but returned about the time stated and
rang the door bell; that Nicholson answered the
bell, and when he reached the door saw Shea
standing with brick in his hand; that he
thereupon drew his revolver and fired through
the door.


The bullet inflicted slight flesh wound on
Shea's neck, but the broken glass and powder
filled his eyes and did more injury than the
bullet. The doctors from the Emergency hos
pital attended Shea, and he afterward re-
moved to his home, No. 325 Maryland avenue
southwest. The shooter was released on 1900
bail.


AFTER THE SHOOTING A RUN-ovER.


After his release Nicholson went out carriage
riding. and when near 18th street and Pennsyl-
vania avenue his horse became unmanageabe
and ran over young man named Stephen A.
Davis and slightly injured him. Nicholson was
then arrested by Officer Weldon, and he left
$40 collateral for his appearance.

FoRr WORTH, TEXAS, Aug. 5.-The south
bound Fort Worth and Denver mail and ex-
press train was robbed by six masked men at 2
o'clock yesterday morning between Cheyenne
and Jascosa, Tex, about 375 miles from Fort
Worth. The passenger coaches were detached
from the locomotive and the engineer forced
to pull his engine ahead few yards and then
walk back and force the express car open with
pick. Express Messenger Marsh, realizing
the situation, concealed all the express pack
ages and put out the lights, and the thieves
secured but three packages of express matter.
which was but a small portion of what was in
the car The mail agent was next compelled to
open his car, and the mail matter was searched
for valuables. The mail agent hid the most
valuable registered packages, and the entire
sum of money secured in both cars will not ex-
ceed $4,000. The passengers were not molested.
After the robbery the bandits ordered the en-
gineer to pull out, and fired a parting shot at
the train. They then made their escape.

San Francisco, Aug. 5.-Dispatches from
Spokane Falls, W. T., say that fire broke out
there at o'ciobk yesterday afternoon and is
burning fiercely. Fears are entertained that
the city will be entirely destroyed. The railroad
depot and the Western Union telegraph Office
are burned, and no particulars can be OBJ

ONLY MEAaER NEWS.


PORTLAND, ORE, Aug. 5.-The last news of
the fire at Spokane Falls was received at
o'clock last evening, when all connection with
that place was lost. Inquiries for news are
coming from all directions, but all that is
known here is that the Northern Pacific depot,
two blocks north, had been burned. and the
Pacific hotel and another block was in fiames
and the wind was tanning the fire toward the
business part of the city.


VIRTUALLY WIPED OUT OF EXISTENCE.


HELENA, MoNT., August 5.-oficials Of the
Western Union telegraph company here are
authority for the statement that Spokane Falls,
w. T.. has been burned to the ground and vir-
tually wiped out of existence. 1t is impossible
to obtain details on account of the interruption
to telegraphic communication. efforts to restore
which are being made, but when success will
be attained it is hard to say.


EVERY BUSINESS house IN THE CITY,
including eight banks, all the hotels but one
all magnificent structures-except the Crescent
block, and every newspaper save the Recie,c
were burned out. The burned district includes
that part of the city from the Northern Pacific
railway to the river and from Lincoln TO Wash
ington streets Several persons are known 10
have perished and several more were injured
by leaping from windows. Charles Davis of
Chicago, a guest at the Arlington house,
was awakened by the flames bursting
through the door of his room on the third
floor. He jumped from the window and was
shocklngiy mangled and died in a few minutes.
woman, whose name is unknown, leaped
from the second story of the Pacific hotel and
was killed The fire spread with such astonishing
rapidity that it is believed many were shut off
from escape before they were even aware of
their danger. dozen large buildings were
blown up with giant powder by the orders
OF the mayor. but even this proved
futile. The Northern Pacific railroad is
probably the heaviest loser, the mag
nihcent new freight warehouse being
destroyed Their loss, including freight burned
will reach about 81, 600 coo. All provisions and
supplies were burned and there viii necessarily
be much suffering for several days. Appeals
for help have been sent out, and Portland
Seattle, Tacoma and several neighboring towns

The battle of North Point was re-fought in
Baltimore yesterday in spite of the mud and
rain. Vice President Morton, Gov. Biggs of
Delaware, Gov. Jackson of Maryland and about
10000 other spectators gathered at Pimlico to
witness the attack. Lieut. l.. S. Bull, in a red
coat, blue trousers and waving plume, repre-
scented Gen. Ross. His death was tragic in the
extreme. After receiving his mortal wound he
clutched his horse wildly around the neck I'M
til lifted of by his aides, who carried him
sadly away. His spirit was afterward noticed
on the club house portico chatting with Mr..
Morton and watching the defeat of his troops.


The American army was arranged in three
lines and Gen. Clinton p. Paine Gen. Smith
commanded them. The British army came
around by the driving park and very mud
splattered army it was that Gen. Ross led upon
the field They didn't looK as if they wanted
to capture Baltimore worth cent; but 10, 900
people had come out in the rain to see them
get whipped. and get whipped they must.
The Washington light infantry were expected
to hold the left of the English advance, but
they did not turn up. The Washington Fenci-
bles, the Union Veteran corps, third battalion
District national guard and the National Rifles
were there, however, and covered themselves
with mud and glory.


For about two hours after Gen. Ross had
fallen the banging of the artillery and the
rattle of rifles, the clouds of smoke and the
evolutions of the soldiers kept up the excite
ment and when at length victory perched upon
the American banner everybody went home
happy in the belief that Baltimore had again
been saved.


Tonight the bombardment of Fort McHenry

CHEYENNE, February 3.-News was
received here to-day Of a singular fatality
by which four Cinnamon lost their lives.
They were in Canyon City, near the yell
lowstone Park, and Yet Sing had estab-
lished wash.house in tent directly
over the boiling spring. He had hot
water constantly on hand and was doing
good business in the new mining town.
On Wednesday he and three other Mon
golians, who came from the mining
camps, celebrated Chinese new year.
They burned fire-crackers and offerings
to Joss, and wound up by getting drunk.
Yet Sing had been cautioned about the
boiling spring and told that it might be
slumbering geyser. For this reason his
wash-tubs were kept on the other side of
the tent, 30 that no soap might disturb
the quiet OF the boiling water. No one
knows how Yet Sings box of laundry
soap got overturned into the boiling
spring, and it is more than probable that
some mischievous miner emptied
the soap into the slum bering gevser.
That night there was sudden spouting
OF boiling water sent flying through the
air and some piercing yells. The miners
rushed up and found the geyser pouring
water to the height of a hundred feet.
The bodies of four Cinnamon, scalded to
death, were found later some distance
from the scene. The geyser spouted for
three hours, and then subsided.

CHICAGO, Jan. 30.-A local paper saws that
while Interstate Commerce Commissioners
Cooley and Morrison were here they made q
searching investigation into the alleged pas
senger irregularities since their last visit
Their inquiry proved a fruitful one. Every
charge made was fully proved, some Of those
inculcated making a clean breast of every-
thing. The ticket deal with Broker Frank re-
vealed some rather unpleasant facts. and
position Mr.. Griffin, until recently local
passenger agent Of the Wabash, showed
that he acted throughout under instruc-
tions from his superior officers, and the COM
missioners exculpated him from any blame in
the matter. Receiver McNulta was before the
commissioners and received quite a severe lee
ture for permitting his subordinstes to engage
In unlawful practices. They felt confident
that Gen. McNulta was not personally respon-
sible, but they thought he should have exer-
cised greater vigilance in the management Of
his passenger department McNulta expressed
regret and assured the commissioners that be
had taken all possible precautions 70 prevent
any irregularities in the future. and that auy
official of his road hereafter detected in wrong
doing would be promptly discharged.


General Passenger Agent Snow was before
the commissioners. The commissioners thought
that there was no excuse for such practices as
he was charged with, and the excuse that be
simply met the competition Of others did not
exonerate him. Because others violated the
law was no reason for him to do likewise. He
was given warning not TO be caught in such
practices again.


General Manager Jeffries, OF the illinois
Central, was broughtbefore the commissioners
and gave valuable evidence. The officials OF
the Burlington and Northern also received an
overhauling for being engaged in practices
that were contrary 20 law. The commission
ers have not yet decided what action they will
take regarding the Developments. They inti-
mate that steps will be taken that will make
similar practices odious in the future. They
will be back again next Monday, when they
may give the matter further consideration

senger train at Berwyn, small station

tive ''killed." Then the robbers began

and messenger fred some twenty shots,

literally riddled the car. The money
stolen is between 5000 and $4,000,
and came principally from Chicago.

The two nurses, one bearing in her arms the
Presidents idol, Benjamin Harrison Mckee,
and the other with the little autocrat's baby
sister, stepped into the vehicle first and then
followed Mrs. Harrison and the President. Sec
rotary WINDOWS carriage was next, and the

ment, and it contained Secretary Rusk, his son,

mia avenue. Recognition of the character of the
parade was quite frequent, and many good

even ragged colored boy standing near the
9Th street approach to the Center market took
off his headgear, which looked like bug-eaten
cabbage leaf, and grinned when the President
smilingly acknowledged his salute.


THE RIDE TO THE MAYNARD
occupied about half an hours time. As the
Presidents carriage rolled under the arched
gateway the three marine corporals who were
on duty thereat fell into line, looking az i'm.
posing as possible, and formally saluted The
same movements were repeated to Secretaries
Window and Rusk and The STAR reporter re-
spectlvely, and then rapid time was made down
the graveled slope and across that portion of
the yard which lntervenes between the COM
mandants headquarters and the wharf, at
which the United States steamer Despatch
was waiting to receive its precious cargo.
There was much blowing of whistles and
footing of bugles when the carriages were
first seen from the vessel; the sailors became
mbued with sudden activity, and the Off
GERS prepared themselves to look befittingly
serious. Albert refined his horses up so that the
carriage door was precisely in line with the
gangway and then Lieut.. Cowles, who is in
command of the Despatch, stepped forward
and, after lifting his cap, assisted Mrs. Harri-
when he had concluded the operation of
shaking hands with the lieutenant ne turned to
the vehicle and lifted out little Benjamin.


LITTLE BENJAMIN AND HIS GRANDFATHER.


Benjamin evidently knew what he was there
for, for he at once started toward the gang
plank Unassisted, he might either have sue
eeeded or failed in his attempt, but he was not
allowed to go too dangerously near the edge,

proffered presidential palm, and with this as
sistance the two celebrities marched between
the double file of ''side-boys' and went on
board. The Mckee baby remained in the car
rriage in its nurses lap, but it made no protest
because it had been sighted. IT looked on
wonderingly, and clapped its little hands and
crowed when the Presidents flag was unfurled
at the main-masthead.

President, and his appearance was the first in
timation the public had that the Connecticut
Senator was going to be of the party.

Just then Commandant Meade signaled a

make any extra preparations. He had been

The guns doomed out their deep-toned re-
spect and the President watched Albert and the
horses. The latter paved three or four times;

port sounded, and while the echoes were play
ing hide and seek over the low-lying Maryland
hills, the President told Commandant Meade

submerged and railroad tracks injured.
Thousands of spectators watchedithe surf,
which was the widest and highest known
in years.


ATLANTIC CITY CUT OFF.
Atlantic City is completely cut off from
the main land, and many bathing houses
are ground up into kindling wood. Sew
eral pavilions were lifted bodily from the
pilings and carried away.


Reports from Coney Island show that
this is the worst encroacbment of the sea
ever known there. All night long the
waves dashed over the breakwater. At
Manhattan and Brighton Beach there
was q tremendous roar. The marine
railway between the two places was en-
tirely swept away. This morning there
was not vestige left of the esplanade in
front of the Manhattan hotel, and the
tide flows in and out of the basement of
the building.


In this city some of the piers are en-
tirely covered by the tide. Some places
usually twelve feet above high water are
licked by the angry waves. The bay and
rivers are exceedingly turbulent, owing
to the high wind. Sailors say it is the
greatest food in twenty years.


FEARS FOR OCEAN STEAMERS.
The storm is believed to have been
right in the track of the ocean steamers
it is feared that some of them, including
the City of New York and Teutonic, have
suffered. Telegraphic communication to
Sandy Hook is cut off. The outside har-
Dor is 90 rough and the weather 80 thick
that boats dare not venture out. Word
comes from Coney Island that the tide
WAS higher this morning than last night.
The Manhattan Beach and Oriental
hotels are flooded to the doors and the
occupants are unable to leave. The
West End Hotel is entirely submerged.
The water is flowing over to Sheepshead
Bay. The beach at Manhattan has been
entirely washed away. Persons still
there are badly frightened.


A Coney Island special says the NAM
moth bathing pavilion belonging to the
Manhattan Beach hotel has been beaten
down by the laundering waves. The old
marine railway was carried away early
| today, and taken with an awful crash
over the new marine railway, fully 300
feet inland, carrying the latter away
bodily, overturning and smashing the
cars like kindling wood. The old
Brighton Beach bathing pavilion fol-
lowed with adeafening crash, and drifted
with herculean force against the new
bath house, tearing part of that away.
The Brighton Beach hotel is surrounded
by over two feet of water. One hundred
feet of the lawn in front of the hotel has
been eaten away since last night, and
will all be gone before tonight. The
Brighton Beach railway is submerged.
No trains are running.


REPORTS FROM UP THE HUDSON


Show that the tide today was the high
est for many years. At Poughkeepsie
the water covered the docks for nearly
100 feet from the usual waters edge. A
severe storm is raging along the river to-
night.


A strong northweHterly gale and the
high tides that have been prevailing for
the last two days have caused great dam
age along the coast of Long island. At
Rockaway Beach the tide reached an un-
paralleled height today. The bathing
houses we're washed away, and the
waves broke in on the verandas of the
hotels. The short stretch of railroad
running between Rockaway Beach, Ar
verne and Far Rockaway was sub.
merged. A portion of it was under.
mined, and the trains had to be- discon-
tinued. The bridge between Arverne
and Rockaway Beach was carried away.


All the small islands in Jamaica bay
were covered with water. Scarcely any,
thing could be seen of Hog island at
high tide. All the buildings on the
island have been washed away. Fire
island and Oak island were cut off from
all communication with the mainland by
boat or telegraph. From the BABYLON
shore great waves could be seen breaking
over both islands during the afternoon,
and it was rumored that four cottages.
occupied by families from Babylon. had
been carried away. An effort was made
to send boat from Babylon to the as.
sistance Of the occupants of the cottages,
but the boat was beaten back by the
wind and tide. At late hour no definite
news has been received concerning their
fate.


Sag Harbor was flooded. Water Gov.

English and had high old time among the
masked bellies. Finally the signal to unmask
was given. and when the masks came off a
great wave OF darkness swept over the hall.
Every blessed man, woman and child in the
place was full-bloOded negro! The drummer
cast one panic-stricken look ut the crowd and
then made for the door. When he reached the
hotel he resumed his old-time personality and
set up the wine.

In Arid Lands.
What nameless boding horror springs
And holds the landscape In Its thrall
Here Death and Terror ever clings.
And Desolation spreads her wings.
And presage OF all evil things
Hangs dark and threatening over all!
How pitiless the suns hot blaze,
Reflected from each splintered peak!
The ufeless plain, the burning rays,
The trackless waste; the mirage haze,
Tell of q land in wrathful days
Spewed up from subterranean deeps!
Like phantom hosts, afar and near,
Ghost-like the shsdowy peaks arise;
Through the faint purple atmosphere,
As those with never hope to cheer,
They seem to shiver as In fear q
Beneath the burning desert SKIES
And yet some Moses rod shall smite-
Some wizards wand shall break the spell
And bring the waters swift to light.
And groves the vision shall delight
And maidens draw the waters bright
Like sweet Rebecca at the well,
Life's pulse again shall throb and thrill
In veins long since parched up and dried;
The sparkling stream its banks shall fill
Sweet ministering angel still,
And glory crown each plain and hill,
And earths long thirst be satisfied.


ALBERT F. KERCHEvAL.

Detective Daniel Coughlin, Patrick O. Sulli-
van. the ice man. and Frank J. Black alias
Woodruff, were indicted by the grand jury In
Chicago last evening for the murder of Dr.
Cronin. This result was reached after an in
vestigation which began at noon and lasted
| seven hours, during which two witnesses were
examined and mass of evidence considered.
The three prisoners were included in one in
dictment. to which there were three counts
one charging them with killing DIR. Cronin
with blunt instrument, the second alleging
the use of sharp instrument and the third in
struments and means unknown.
No evidence was introduced to prove a con-
splracy, and DR.. Cronin's private papers were
not placed before the grand jury. The wit
nesses called were those whose stories have
been told in general outline, if not in detail
In the press. Judge Longenecker thought it
advisable to tighten the coils into which the
three prisoners had already been drawn. and
fasten them with indictments, probably to pre-
vent any attempt to secure the release of one
or more of them on bail


Woodruff is the man who saws he carried a
body IN wagon to Lincoln park on the night
of DIR. Cronin's disappearance


The jury took only one vote after hearing
the witnesses. and that was unanimous for
lndlctlnS All three prisoners. States Attorney
LonSenecker said tonight that no mention of
Clan-na-Gael affairs had been made in the iurv
room. The charge of conspiracy was not in
vestigated, ;" he added, land Dir. Cronin's papers
were not brought in. Those matters will come
later, probably before another grand jury"


THE CoROSERs INQUEST.


The coroner took the jury out to the cottage
to view the place where the murder was COM
mitted, to the catch-basin where the body was
found, and over the route taken by the wagon
Ill which the body was taken after it left the
Carlson cottage. The jury is an intelligent one.
They started out In carriages, and after taking
IN Lieut.. SpeDgler at the Lake View police
station. they went to the cottage, at No 1872
Ashland avenue, where the murder was done.
The jury noted the steps where blood-stains
had turned them a dirty brown. They went
into the front room, saw the rudely-painted
floor daubed crude mud-colOr. examined the
footprints from the fresh yellow paint on the
purplish red of the hall and bedroom floors,
examined carefully spots of blood in the center
of the floor. and scrutinizing with eyeglasses
the splotches of blood on the wall where the
llfe-tlde had spurted when the assassin struck
the blow.


THE TELL-TALE LAMP.


A fresh discovery was made yesterday. and
that is that the handle of the lamp was smeared
with the yellow ochre. showing that the floor
had been painted after dark, probably immedi-
ately after the murder.


From the cottage the party drove out Evans





where the bloody trunk was found Thence
the party drove half mile farther on to the
man-hole, where the doubled up body of the
murdered doctor was found Lifting up the
lid, Lieut.. Spengler pointed out the cotton bat
ting still sticking to the splinters of the rough
wood frame work.


1T is this gentlemen of the Jury" said Cor
oner Hertz. pointing to the thin fluffs. now
grayed by moisture. lit is this which connects
the body of DIR. Cronin found here with the
trunk mystery and the cottage. for the trunk
bottom was covered with cotton and there were
tufts of IT found in the cottage


After viewing this the jury returned to Chicago
at O'Clock and the further investigation was
deferred until this morning at 10 O'Clock.


BRUCEs UNLIKELY STORY.


Detective Robert Bruce, who has been con-
Quoting private agency i'll Chicago, walked
into Lieut.. Horace Elliott's office Yesterday
morning and said that several months ago AL
derman Mccormack offered him 81 100 to kill
DIR; Cronin. Bruce, who has just returned from
a three months stay In Texas, saws that McCor-
mack paid him 800 in advance. and agreed to
pay the remaining $1,000 when the lob was
done. Bruce declares that Mccormack told
him to feign sickness in his office. and then
send for DIR. Cronin and kill him Bruce saws
he took the 800, spent it for liquor, and
never made move toward carrying out the
contract


Bruce bears a rather unsavory reputation,
and the ponce do not place all the reliance in
the world in his story

Three boys who escaped from the reformatory
farm, at Salem, Mass, Wednesday, had a thrill
ing experience while crossing the harbor. They
made raft by mailing a board across three
short logs and then launched their fragile
craft. The wind was blowing off shore, and
was sufficiently strong to raise ugly white caps
The raft went to pieces in few minutes and
each boy seized a log. They were rolled under
by every wave. and the two younger lads were
nearly drowned. The oldest of the trio named
Hurley, padded about until he had pushed the
logs together. Then he laid down fiat upon
the logs and kept them together by extending
his legs and arms across them, getting grip
with his hands and feet. The water broke over
him repeatedly. but his presence Of mind alone
saved the entire party from drowning. Another
boy, Kennedy, stood In water to his knees, and.
by dint Of hard padding with board, sue
eeeded in stemming the current and landing
Just below the lighthouse at Hospital Point,
Beverly side. They struck out for Gloucester,
but were captured.

A marriage which was to have taken place at
Camden. n. j., was interrupted Sunday night
in an unexpected way. The contracting parties,
Henry Brown and Miss Mary Morgan, stood
before the Rev. MIR. Clayton, preparatory to
becoming man and wife. A portion of the
service had been already read, about fifty wit
nesses being present, when the bride uttered a
loud scream All eyes were Immediately fixed
upon her. She was seen to raise her hand and
point toward corner of the church. The mex,
moment she fell to the floor in a swoon and
had to be carried out. Physicians worked with
her for nearly an hour before she was restored
to consciousness. When fully recovered she
gave curious explanation of her conduct
Her mother, who died four months ago, was
opposed to her marriage with Brown. The
marriage was for 4 time delayed, but after Mrs.
Morgans death arrangements for it were
pushed. Miss Morgan says that Just when she
was about to pronounce the binding words she
raised her eyes and saw her mothers ghost
then she tainted. The wedding was postponed
for several days.

The most thoroughly pumped members that
ever graced the House of Representatives were
those who ventured outside the hall while the
caucus was in progress. hundred waiting
newspaper men voraciously pounced upon them
and endeavored to find out all they knew, and
when they got that they were not satisfied
Every man was, for the time being an Oliver
Twist and every man cried for more. The cor
respondents and reporters were shut out of
their gallery lest they might overhear some of
the proceedings, and they had to do a good
deal OF hustling not only to get the news but
to write it and get it on the wires. Competi-
tion in this respect was very keen.


THE REED MEN


started into the caucus with the hope of draw
ing the desired votes from some of the other
candidates. One Of the leading Reed men said
to STAR reporter that they could have had
four more votes than enough to elect their can
didate, but that they refused to make the bar
gain that was necessary to accomplish this
They were pledged to the support of Wheat of
Wisconsin for door keeper, and they would not
throw him over for Adams to get the southern
votes, which would have elected him. Conse-
quently, he said Reed would not get more than
i've of the southern votes.


The New York delegation met in the terri
tories committee room just before the caucus
assembled and by unanimous vote ipdorsed
Wheat Of Wisconsin for doorkeeper.


OPENING PROCEEDINGS.


The caucus was called to order few minutes
after noon by Representative McComas of
Maryland, the secretary Of the caucus commit
tee of the last House.


Gen. Henderson Of Illinois having been
chosen chairman call Of the roll was begun
TO determine how many were present


The call Of the roll showed that one hundred
and sixty-fve Of the one hundred and sixty-
nine republican representatives were present
Vi the aosentees IL was understood three are
pieoged TO Heed and one to Mckinley.

The delegations came into the House before
the caucus solid for their respective candidates.
The western men were combined and conf
dent. Probably half a dozen Of them
felt that Reed was going to be elected.
but in the face of this conviction declared
that they would stand by their own
candidates until the Speaker was elected.
All they needed to defeat the Maine candidate
was to be as solid as they said they were. Each
candidate in the western combination was sure
Of holding his own forces, but was anxious
about the supporters of the other candidates.
Members crowded the republican side of the
House before IL o'clock and in three minutes


RUMoRs OF ALL SORTS


were flying about. The Reed men were hunt
ing for the fourteen votes necessary for his
election. To secure these reports were sent
whirling to the effect that this or that delega-
tion was going to break from the west.


These reports were promptly denied when
they reached the ears of the men they related
to. Not only that but those men whose firm
ness was questioned were the madest men to

EUREKA, CAL, November 16.-The
tugs Buhne, Ranger, Mary Ann and
Sprinter left the harbor at an early hour
this morning, and after the Ranger had
crossed the bar, and when in four faith
oms of water, she was struck by heavy
sea, which started her house and dis
abled her smokesteck, at the same time
washing John d. Rogers, deck hand,
overheard. He was not seen afterward.
The bar was not unusually rough, but
the seas outside were heavy and struck
with great violence. The Ranger re.
turned into the bay soon after the acci-
dent.


An hour later the tug Sprinter, which
had been several miles off shore, came
up to the bar with the schooner Fidelity
in tow. The tug crossed without taking
any water, but just as the schooner had
reached the inner edge of the bar, heavy
sea caught her under the port quarter,
broaching her far to windward and send
ing her over with all on board. The tug
held on to the capsized vessel for more
than half an hour, but finding both were
drifting into the breakers, was obliged to
cut the hawser, Not one Of the men on
the ill.fated craft was seen after she cap.
sized. The crew consisted of the captain
and seven men, and the vessel was just
returning from voyage to Santa Bar.
bara.


Captain Christopher was we'll known
here, and it is understood his wife is in
this city. At last accounts the vessel
was drifting toward Eel river. The
disaster occurred at high water, and it is
likely the bodies of the lost sailors were
carried to sea.

Steamers Are Drowned.


MONTREAL, May 22.-The steamships
Cynthia and Polynesian collided this
morning near Long Point, few miles
east. Eight lives are reported lost. The
| Cynthia was freighter, inward-bound
from Glasgow. The Polynesian was out
ward bound with freight and passe ngera
for Liverpool. Immediately after the
collision the Cynthia sank in twelve
fathoms. The survivors from the Cynthia
swan ashore. The Polynesian proceeded
to Quebec in damaged condition. The
collision of the steamers was the result
of a misunderstanding of signals for pass
ing at dangerous curve in the channel.
The following is list of the crew of the
Cynthia who lost their lives


Hugh Irving, chief cook; Alexander
Nicholas, sailor; Andrew Vance, trim
mer; Charles McCracken, trimmer; /;
James Low, fireman; James Ferron,
boatswain; Charles Blackstock, mess
room boy; David Young, a stowaway
from Glasgow.


The blame is laid at the door of the
Polynesian, and her officers are much
blamed for not stopping to render assist.
ance.


The sailors of the Cynthia claim that
the Polynesian steamed right ahead, and
that, had she stopped, she could have
saved the men who were drowned. They
also state that there were fifteen men on
shore, who, although there were boats
near by, did not raise f1ger in an at
tempt to rsscue the drowning sailors.


The pilot on the Cynthia says the Poly.
nesian was not in her proper course, and
to this he ascribes the collision. The
weather WAS perfectly clear, and those on
board the Cynthia were surprised to see
the course the Polynesian was making
Instead of coming straight down the
channel, she was crossing the course OF
the Cynthia, which was, agreeably to
the marine law, keeping on the starboard
side of the river. When fifty feet away
the Polynesian blew her whistle to signal
the Cynthia to take the opposite
side of the channel. The pilot accord
ingly put her about and endeavored to
cross but, seeing it could not be done,
signalled to have the engines reversed.
1t was vain effort and the next minute
the vessels had met. After the collision
the Polynesian kept on her course. The
Captain on the Cynthia tried to run that





most Immediately she capsized
sideways, and all tried to
make their escape as best they could.
One man was crushed to death at the
time of the collision, and seven were
drowned while attempting to reach shore.
The mariners say it was impossible for
the Polynesian to render the Cynthia
any assistance. With the "way" Oh her,
caused by her full speed down stream,
she could not have stopped, and, even if
she could have stopped in short dis
tance, she would have been unable to
turn.


QUEBEC, May %. The steamship
Polynesian arrived here safely this even
ing. She has received serious damage,
the extent OF which cannot be known
until the surveyors have made their re-
port.

Miss Nina Trevelyan and her sister Mamie,
two young girls. left their residence, near Nor
folk, Va, a few days ago, accompanied by gen.
tleman friend, on a wild goose and duck expe-
dition in the bay. Both ladies were familiar
with the use of shot guns and anticipated q
pleasant time. At o'clock they procured
sail boat and sped across the bay, where the
blinds where ready for occupancy. After sun
game, they hoisted sail and endeavored to make
the landing from which they embarked The
night was very dark, and they were on the east
ern side OF the Chesapeake. When they started
that it had changed to several points to the
south and lost their reckoning. For hours they
beat up and down the chesapeake, lost, as il
in mid-ocean. The night was bitter cold, and
the gale high, but the girls never expressed any
heavy blankets that had been used for
blinds. No sign Of human habitation
or civilization hove in sight until after
midnight, when their craft ran into
lot OF anchored skiis. This brought them to
posed to the weather, they discovered . little
cabin. in which they found plenty Of wood,
and soon had q cracking FIRE, but it was q long
time before the half-frozen ladies recovered.
much persuasion. were induced to try to get a
little sleep. Suddenly piercing scream came
from Miss Nina, who sprang to the center Of
the cabin. The other young lady frightened
almost to death, sprang from her bunk, re-
ceiving several severe Commissions and at the
same time adding her soprano to the music.
The trouble was explained when the younger
one exclaimed, rats" Investigation proved
that horde of marsh rats had entered the
cabin and sought refuge under the blankets
and pillows. At daybreak Sunday sail was
hoisted and, after securing the bay shore for
hours, they finally discovered their landing,
arriving home late that evening. The girls
were received with open arms by their parents,
who had given them up for lost.

GRAFTON, OAK, July 20.-Dry, hot winds in
portions Of the extreme north Dakota, near the
boundary line, have played havoc with the
crops, and farmers are reduced to eating field
rodents, gophers, &C., for subsistence.


The crop in the Canadian northwest will be
nil. A party Of emigrants arrived yesterday
from the Souris country. They had travelled
800 miles through well-settled country on the
Canadian side without seeing fair crop, and
say great many settlers are leaving their land
to drive their cattle to timbered country on
this side.


Some of the families looked famine stricken
and had eaten nothing but potatoes and turnips
for some months. They were afflicted with
scurvy and were sacrificing themselves to save
their cattle. At one place, northwest from Tur-
tie mountains, family of English emigrants.
who were travelling back to the mountains had
killed and were eating young colt. The suf-
fering in that isolated region will be awful,
and those who have means will leave in such
numbers as to depopulate the Canadian north
west. They are new settlers in that country
and have no resource but the wheat crop.

LONDON, July 20.-A Berlin dispatch to-day
reports that the police prosecution of the two
editors Holdheim, and Bernstein, Of the we'll
known socialistic daily the Vols Zeit,ing and
the director, Franz May, has fallen through,
and that the prisoners have been discharged
The Volts Zeituag is a newspaper with q circu-
lation Of nearly $4,000, but In politics it is bit
terly opposed to Bismarck. One fine day last
March the iron chancellor found in its columns
an uncomplimentary reference to himself. and
had the police at once suppress the paper
under the act directed against the socialists.
The following day the VOks Zeit,uag did not
appear, but paper Of exactly the same size,
shape and general appearance did appear from
the same Office with the title The WorL,ersndrf.


THE TWELVE WISE POLICE INSPECTORS


got together, carefully adjusted their specta-
c.es and after a thorough examination Of the
fedgeling decided it was only the VoH-s Zeitung
with a nom, ordered its suppression. With q
profound veneration for the law and the police,
the management of the paper did not publish
the Workersn0rt, but the next days paper was
called the Future. This the police as promptly
suppressed, but when on the following day the
same paper appeared with brand new name the
police gave up in despair, foreseeing that the
editors could practically set their edcts at de-
hance 80 long as their list of new names held
out, and this promised to prove mex
haustible. The director, Herr May, and
the two editors, Herren Holdheim and
Bernstein, were thereupon arrested, charged
with the serious offense of publishing news
paper after its publication had been forbidden
under the law by the proper authorities. OF
course the whole question for the court to de-
eide was whether a newspaper, after its name
had been changed, could or could not properly
be considered the same newspaper. The pros
ecuting attorney insisted that to all intents and
purposes the Volts Zeitc1g was really published
after its prohibition, even though the name was
changed, while counsel for the defense urged
that this was forced and


TYRANNIcAL CONSTRUCTION OF THE LAW.


After listening to the arguments of counsel
on both sides yesterday the court decided that
the newspapers published under different til
ties could not be considered as the same news
paper, and accordingly the prisoners were dis
charged When the three men left the court
room they were received with loud huzzahs by
their sympathizers outside, who thronged the
approaches to the chamber and carried the
three men on their shoulders for several
blocks. 1t is now stated that the police by
daily suppressions will compel the editors to
change the name of their paper every day.

Hope, Alaska, October 8, 1888. The details Of
the wreck are now learned for the first time.
Lisburne was sighted on the morning Of Octo-
Der 5. The day was windy, and toward evening
one OF the worst storms ever experienced in
that region came up. About Q o'clock the bark
struck near Point Hope, but a. the air was

iceberg had been struck. The vessel seemed
70 be rapidly going to pieces, and Capt. George
7. Allen ordered the first mate to cut away the
masts. This was the last order given by the
captain, as he was never seen again, the heavy
sea carrying him overheard

were % strong it was impossible for the men,

hold on the masts and rigging, and they were
thrown to the mercy Of the roaring waters,

board, and but eight now survive. Most of the
men were frozen so stiff they could not keep
themselves above the water and persisted be-
fore the vessel went to pieces.


Alexander Omey gave up hope while on the
vessel and killed himself with his pistol. The
first mate, Thomas +. Pease, and second mate,

the tune Of 50 miles an hour. In shipping circles

in this morning with tales Of high seas and
terrible weather.

The White Star steamer Teutonic, which left
Queenstown with the City Of New York, was
one OF the first steamers to pass Sandy Hook
this morning, followed soon afterward by
the Pennland, from Antwerp; the Rot
terdam, from Rotterdam, and the Hammonia,
from Hamburg. Each vessel reports having
experienced unusually heavy weather, but had
met with no serious trouble. About 9 o'clock
the Roanoke and Richmond of the old Dominion
line arrived. They, too, had had their share of
rough weather, which was shown by their
smoke stacks and rigging. The Roanoke left
Norfolk last Monday night She was due
here at 10 o'clock Tuesday night. The
captain reports that while his YES
sci sustained no serious damage,
the trip was one of the toughest he had ever
experienced. From the time he left until his
arrival storm after storm was encountered with
but little recess between.


SOUGHT SAFETY IN aRAvRsEND BAY.


The Richmond, which should now be on her
way south, having started last Tuesday night,
put back. The storm was encountered of the
light ship about midnight Tuesday, and fear
full of venturing further to sea the
anchor was left down in Gravesend bay See
ing that the storm showed no sign Of abating,
and as the vessel was light, the captain turned
her nose back toward her dock. The weather
In the lower bay, the captain says. was I'M
precedentedly severe. The wind blew at q
terrific rate, while, strange to say, dense fog
enyeloped everything and made navigation
well nigh impossible. Gravesend bay, he
added, was covered with steamers and vessels

warmer than usual generally throughout all
agricultural regions east of the Mississippi. The
weather was generally favorable for growing
crops in all districts except Tennessee, Missis-
sippi and TexaS, where excessive rams caused
some damage to wheat and cotton In the
spring wheat region of Minnesota and Dakota

the principal corn states, including illinois,
Indiana, Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska, the
weather was favorable and corn has made rapid
growth during the week. In Michigan and
Ohio the growth Of corn has been retarded
owing to continued wet weather. The harvest
ing Of wheat, barley and clover il in progress
a. far north as the central portions Of Ohio,
Indiana and Illinois, but work has been retarded
by frequent rains, and in some sections har-
vested crops slightly injured by rains. Reports
from kentucky state that the tobacco crop is
excellent The high temperature and general
rains In Louisiana were very favorable and
doubtless greatly improved the corn, cane and
rice crops In the east and central portions of
the cotton region all crops were favorsbiy
Affected; the wheat harvest il about completed

In Pennsylvania the heavy rains were unfayor-
able for ripening grain and embarrassing,

SAN Francisco, January 1O.-The fight
Golden Gate Athletic Club last night, be-
tween the light weights Billy Mahan, of
California, and George Mulholland, of
Australia, was the longest ever fought on
this coast. The battle commenced at
8 40 O'Clock and continued until 8 :25 this
morning when it was declared draw at
the close of the eighty seventh round.
Joe McAuliffe, who was recently
defeated by Peter Jackson, was referee.
Throughout the fight Mulholland
showed himself superior in science and
quickness, but Mahan exhibited all the
qualities Of game and hard fighter.
About the fiftieth round it seemed al
most certain that Mulholland would win,
as he had been punished very little,
while Mahan's lips and cheeks were
badly swollen, his eyes nearly closed
and he had lost one tooth by contact with
the Australians head. However, Mulhol-
land did not seem to be able to give the
knock out blow, and during the last
two hours of the fight Mahan was as
fresh as his antagonist and administered
some severe punishment on Mulholland's
wind. Both men slipped and fell to the
floor several times during the battle, but
the only clean knock-down was in the
ffty-second round. when Mulholland was
sent under the ropes by terrific blow
in the stomach. After it became appar-
ent that neither of the men was likely to
be knocked out, there were numerous
demands for draw, and the referee
| finally consented to the proposition, after
the battle had lasted five hours and
three-quarters, and when both men were
too weak to strike an effective blow.

tered places and fired signal guns every few

women were found

The weather-crop bulletin of the signal Office
says: The week ending July was slightly
warmer than usual generally throughout the
northern states, while the temperature differed
but slightly from the normal over the cotton
and tobacco regions of the southern states.
There was more rain than usual during the
week throughout all states on the Atlantic
coast from New York to Florida, and in the
gulf states from Georgia to western Texas
Over the greater portion of this region the rain
fall exceeded inches, while in North Carolina
and southern Alabama over inches fell. Ex-
cessive rains are also reported in many locali-
ties in the Mississippi valley from Cairo north
ward to Wisconsin, and in northern Minnesota,
including the Red River valley. Over the
greater portion of the principal wheat and corn
states, however, the rainfall was less than usual
and the high temperature, with more than the
average amount of sunshine, was doubtless
favorable to the growing crops and harvest
work. The weather has been especially favor
able for growing crops throughout the corn
and wheat belt. The crops are reported as
growing rapidly, especially corn and winter
wheat harvest is well under way with a good
yield reported

Santa Fe train was pulling out of Crowley, 10
miles south Of this city, three men boarded

motive. The two on the engine placed pistols
to the heads of Engineer Monohan and Fireman
Crager, and told them to pull out and stop
when told. When two miles from Crowley the
engineer was ordered to stop. Then the rob-
bers cut the engine, baggage, mail and express
cars from the rest of the train and made Mono.
han pull half q mile further.

messenger to show them the money. He
pointed to three bags Of Mexican silver. One
Of the men ripped open sack and shoveled
the silver out Of the door, while the other one
threw out the other sacks. They took two
packages said to contain $1,000 each, but over
looked three or four money packages for Fort
Worth. The short man finally ordered those
with him to let the two full sacks alone. The
engineer was then made to couple up and move.

SAN FRANCISCO, October 16.-Billy
Hennesy, Of Kansas City, was knocked
out in the forty.fifth round at the Colder
Gate Club tonight by Charles Turner, Of
Stockton, in fight for purse of $3.50
The fight was game one from the start
but the negro's repeated jabbing in Hen
nesy's wind and on his jaw, which the
latter could not prevent, gradually threw
him out of condition. Hennesy
was knocked down in the seventh round
but in the thirty-sixth he got in pivotal
swing on the Stockton mans cheek that
nearly knocked him out.


Beginning with the thirty-fourth round
some fierce fighting occurred, Turner
rushing wildly with his right and left.
He received blow in the wind, how
ever, that caused him to groan with
pain. He rushed Hennesy into his cor
ner, and drove blow upon blow into the
latter's face, knocking him nearly under
the ropes.


In the forty-frst Hennesy slipped dur.
ing clinch, and the negro drove him
around with his head down, striving to
knock him out. The fight was almost
continuous from now till the close. Hen
messy, by backhand blow in the forty
second, tried to knock the Stocktonian
down. He left himself open and Turner
forced him to his knees, and when he
arose Hennesy was apparently gone.
Hennesy was weakening, and caught
the negro by the legs time and again,
seeking to save himself from the terrible
jabs the negro dealt him.


In the last round Turner gave him a
severe left-hander in the mouth, bring
ing blood and causing his lips to swell.
Hennesy went down, but rose as eight
seconds were counted. Turner bounced
on him, driving him to the ropes and
uppercutting him. The fight was over.
Hennesy fell, and though he made a
brave effort to rise, was counted out.

Britannia, Captain Dawson, from New-York Sep
tember for Liverpool, which arrived at Queens
town to-day, reports that on the morning of Sep
tember fire broke out in the cotton slowed
under of the port matches. All the passengers
except a few sturdy men from the steerage were
kept away from the fire by lines stretched across
the ship. The officers and crew, assisted by the
selected steerage passengers then worked with
skill and energy to extinguish the flames. A num-
Der of bales Of the burning cotton were thrown
overheard and remained in the water for two
hours after which they were picked up and slowed

was drenched.

serious conflict is feared Two years after

turn the collections and pew rents over to the
pastor. The archbiship then issued to Father

deavored to smooth matters over, and sue
ceeded- Everything went well until few
weeks ago, when the rebellious few gained the
ascendancy once more. The pastor read the
archbishop's letter from the pulpit, and q
stormy scene followed. Father Kobrzynski
finally left the church, fearing personal
violence.


Last Saturday the entire matter was laid be-
fore Archbishop Feehan, when the trustees OF
the church were directed to resign their trusts.
This they refused to do and the archbishop in
masses. On Sunday Father Kobrzynski as
cended the pulpit and announced the edict OF

murmur swept through the congregation,

floor with their feet others threw their rituals
over their heads, while still others left the
church. In the middle of all this the
pastor began to say mass. When it became APP
parent that no solemn high mass was to be
celebrated men, women and children focked
down the central aisle of the church in wild
disorder. For moment the pastor, undis-
mayed by the taunts and threats of his flock,
continued his holy Office. When, however, in
the middle Of the mass, the wofshipers left
their seats and scrambled pell-mell over the
fearing mob violence, rushed from the altar
and out through the parsonage way. He was
secreted for several hours by personal friends,
who feared that the excited people would use
him roughly if they laid their hands on him. II
is expected that the archbishop will deal
